Mangrove forests occupy less than one percent of the world's tropical land, yet the mud beneath them holds a disproportionate share of coastal carbon. Because the roots trap fine sediment and the waterlogged soil contains little oxygen, dead leaves and roots decompose very slowly, and carbon accumulates for centuries. When a mangrove is cleared for a shrimp pond, the exposed soil dries and oxidises, releasing in a few years carbon that took several centuries to store. For this reason, some ecologists argue that protecting an existing mangrove is worth more, in climate terms, than planting a new one of the same area: the new forest begins with an empty carbon account, whereas the old one is defending centuries of savings.

Based only on the passage, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Shrimp farming is the main cause of mangrove loss across the world.
The slow decay of plant matter in mangrove soil is linked to the soil having little oxygen.
Mangrove forests cover more than one percent of the world's tropical land.
A newly planted mangrove stores more carbon in its first years than an old mangrove of the same area.
solution:
The second sentence links slow decomposition to waterlogged soil that "contains little oxygen": (B) paraphrases it.
(C) contradicts "less than one percent".
(D) contradicts "the new forest begins with an empty carbon account".
(A) is out of scope: shrimp ponds are one example of clearing, not ranked as the main cause anywhere.

The author describes an old mangrove as "defending centuries of savings" in order to suggest that
options: mangroves are economically more valuable than shrimp ponds
the carbon in mangrove soil grows every year like interest on a deposit
planting new mangroves is of no use in climate terms
losing an old mangrove gives up stored carbon that a new planting cannot quickly replace

(A) reads the money metaphor literally; the passage compares climate value, not profit.
(C) is too strong: the passage says protecting is worth more, not that planting is useless.
(B) pushes the metaphor too far; nothing is said about compounding.

q:
More than nine-tenths of the data that crosses oceans travels through cables lying on the seabed. In deep water, where little can disturb it, a modern cable is barely thicker than a garden hose; near the shore, where ship anchors and fishing trawlers are a threat, it is armoured with steel wire and often buried. Even so, faults are far more common in shallow water than in the deep ocean. Repairing one is slow: a specialised ship must sail to the site, grapple the cable from the bottom, haul it aboard and splice in a new section. Operators therefore protect themselves less by making cables stronger than by laying several cables along different routes, so that traffic can be shifted when one fails.

Which one of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?
options: Cables in deep water are armoured because repairs there are the most difficult.
Repairing a damaged cable involves lifting it from the seabed.
Laying cables along several routes lets traffic continue when one cable is damaged.
A cable fault close to a coast is more likely than one far out at sea.
solution:
The passage says the deep-water cable is "barely thicker than a garden hose" and that armour is used near the shore, so (A) contradicts it.
(D) restates "faults are far more common in shallow water".
(C) restates the last sentence.
(B) restates "grapple the cable from the bottom, haul it aboard".

q:
When onion prices spiked after an unseasonal flood, the state capped the retail price at ₹40 a kilogram. Shoppers were relieved for a week. Then the shelves emptied. Traders who had bought stock at ₹45 a kilogram from wholesalers could not sell at ₹40 without a loss, so they sent their onions to neighbouring states where no cap applied. Those who did sell at the official price found that buyers bought far more than they needed, fearing that supplies would vanish. By the end of the month, the onion that was officially cheap was, for most households, simply unavailable, and a quiet market had sprung up behind shop counters where onions changed hands at ₹70 a kilogram.

Which one of the following best captures the central point of the passage?
options: Consumers should not buy more food than they need during a shortage.
Onions sold in neighbouring states were costlier than those sold in the state.
A price cap set below the cost of supply can make a good scarcer rather than cheaper.
Floods are the main reason why onion prices rise sharply.
solution:
Everything in the passage traces how a cap of ₹40 (below the traders' cost of ₹45) emptied shelves and pushed onions into a ₹70 hidden market: the "cheap" onion became unavailable. That is (C).
(D) is out of scope: the flood is only the trigger.
(B) is not stated: no price is given for the neighbouring states.
(A) moralises about one detail (over-buying); it is not the author's point.

q:
Long before piped water, the dry western regions of India relied on stepwells: deep trenches lined with stone stairs that led down to the water table. Because the level of groundwater rose and fell with the seasons, a user in the monsoon might stop on an upper landing, while in summer the same user walked several storeys down. Builders turned this necessity into art, adding carved pillars and shaded pavilions at each landing, which made the wells cool gathering places as well as sources of water. Many stepwells fell into disuse in the colonial period, when the authorities, alarmed by the stagnant water, preferred pumps and pipes. Some of the neglected wells are now being cleaned and restored, more as monuments than as water supplies.

Based only on the passage, which one of the following can be inferred?
options: How far a user had to climb down a stepwell depended on the season.
The colonial authorities demolished most of the stepwells.
Stepwells were built only in the western regions of India.
Restored stepwells now supply most of the drinking water in these regions.
solution:
The groundwater level "rose and fell with the seasons", so a monsoon user stopped on an upper landing and a summer user went several storeys down: (A).
(C) is too strong: the passage says western regions relied on them, not that they existed nowhere else.
(B) upgrades "fell into disuse" into demolition.
(D) contradicts "more as monuments than as water supplies".

q:
City planners in a hot inland town have proposed painting the roofs of all municipal buildings white. White roofs reflect most of the sunlight that falls on them, whereas dark roofs absorb it and release it as heat. The planners argue that the scheme will lower indoor temperatures in these buildings and therefore cut the municipality's spending on air-conditioning by a noticeable amount. Critics reply that municipal buildings make up only a small fraction of the town's roof area, so the effect on the town's overall temperature will be negligible. The planners do not dispute this; their claim, they say, was never about the town as a whole.

The planners' argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?
options: White paint is cheaper than the paint now used on the roofs.
Private owners will also paint their roofs white once the scheme succeeds.
Painting the municipal roofs white will lower the temperature of the whole town.
Lower indoor temperatures in the municipal buildings would lead to less use of air-conditioning in them.
solution:
Chain: white roof → cooler interior → lower air-conditioning spending. The second link is unstated. Negate (D) (cooler rooms do not reduce air-conditioning use) and the conclusion about spending collapses, so it is the assumption.
(A) is irrelevant: the cost of paint is not part of the claim.
(C) is a claim the planners explicitly disown ("never about the town as a whole").
(B) is outside the argument, which concerns municipal buildings only.

q:
A generation ago, the typical visitor to a public library came to borrow a book. Today, in many towns, the busiest corner of the library is not the shelves but the row of desks with power sockets and free internet. Students preparing for competitive examinations occupy them from opening to closing time, many of them coming from homes too small or too noisy for sustained study. Librarians who once measured their success by the number of books lent now find that lending has fallen even as daily footfall has risen. Some councils, looking only at the falling loan figures, have proposed cutting library budgets, a decision that would penalise precisely the users who depend most on the space.

The author's attitude towards the proposal to cut library budgets is best described as
options: nostalgic, because the author wants libraries to return to lending books
indifferent, because students can find other places to study
approving, because fewer books are being lent than before
critical, because the proposal relies on a measure that misses how libraries are now used
solution:
Key phrases: councils look "only at the falling loan figures"; the cut "would penalise precisely the users who depend most on the space". The author objects that loans are the wrong measure when footfall has risen: (D).
(C) reverses the author's stance.
(B) contradicts the concern for users from homes "too small or too noisy".
(A) misreads the opening contrast; the author defends the new use of the space, not a return to lending.

q:
Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and must reach the sea quickly, before crabs and birds find them. They do not see the sea as such; they move toward the brightest part of the horizon, which on a natural beach is the open water reflecting starlight and moonlight. Along coasts lit by hotels and street lamps, the brightest horizon is often inland. Hatchlings there crawl away from the water, and many die of exhaustion or are crushed on roads. Conservationists have found that simple measures, such as shielding lights so that they point downward or using amber lamps that hatchlings are less drawn to, can restore normal behaviour without plunging the coast into darkness.

Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: On a beach where the land behind the nests is brighter than the sea, hatchlings would tend to move away from the sea.
Hatchlings are unable to see amber light.
Most hatchlings on unlit beaches survive to adulthood.
Coastal hotels are legally required to switch off their lights at night.
solution:
The passage gives the rule: hatchlings move toward the brightest part of the horizon. Apply it: if the land is brighter, they head inland, away from the sea: (A).
(B) is too strong: amber lamps are ones hatchlings are "less drawn to", not invisible to them.
(C) is out of scope: survival to adulthood is never discussed.
(D) is out of scope: no law is mentioned, and the remedy is shielding, not switching off.

q:
As cockpit automation improved, accidents caused by routine pilot error fell sharply. Yet investigators began to notice a different pattern. When automation failed suddenly, because of a frozen sensor or a disconnected autopilot, pilots who had spent most of their flying hours monitoring screens sometimes struggled to fly the aircraft by hand. The very reliability of the system had made the rare moments of manual control both more critical and less practised. Some airlines have responded by requiring pilots to fly a share of their routine flights manually, accepting a small loss of efficiency in exchange for skills that may be needed only once in a career.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
options: Airlines Abandon Cockpit Automation
A History of Aviation Safety
When Reliable Machines Weaken Human Skill
Why Autopilots Fail
solution:
The passage argues that reliable automation leaves pilots short of practice for the rare moments it fails, and describes the airlines' remedy: (C) covers the whole.
(D) is too narrow and mis-focused: causes of failure are mentioned only in passing.
(B) is too broad.
(A) is extreme: airlines add some manual flying; they do not abandon automation.

pilots prefer flying by hand to monitoring screens

A potato farmer who must sell his crop on the day it is harvested has little power over the price. Every farmer in the district is harvesting at the same time, traders know that the potatoes will rot within weeks, and the price at harvest is therefore the lowest of the year. A farmer with access to cold storage faces a different market. He can wait until the glut clears and sell when prices recover, and the mere fact that he can wait strengthens his hand in bargaining even if he chooses to sell at once. The benefit of cold storage, in other words, does not lie only in the potatoes it preserves.

Which one of the following best expresses the point of the last sentence of the passage?
options: Farmers with cold storage always get the highest price of the year.
Cold storage reduces the quantity of potatoes that rot after harvest.
Cold storage benefits traders more than it benefits farmers.
The ability to delay a sale improves a farmer's bargaining position even when he does not delay.
solution:
"Does not lie only in the potatoes it preserves" points to the benefit just described: the option to wait "strengthens his hand … even if he chooses to sell at once": (D).
(B) is the obvious benefit the sentence says is not the only one; it is not the point being made.
(A) is extreme ("always", "highest").
(C) is out of scope and reverses whom the passage says is helped.

Before railways, every town kept its own time, set by the sun at local noon. A town a few hundred kilometres to the east was some minutes ahead, and nobody minded, because no one travelled fast enough to notice. Railways changed that. A timetable listing departures in a dozen local times was an invitation to missed connections and, worse, to collisions on single-track lines where two trains relied on knowing which would reach a passing loop first. Railway companies therefore adopted a single standard time along their lines, and towns, finding it inconvenient to live by two clocks, gradually followed. Uniform time, which now seems a natural fact, began as an operating rule of a transport business.

Which one of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Towns were compelled by law to adopt the time used by the railways.
Railway collisions were caused mainly by clocks that showed the wrong time.
Uniform time came about largely because of the practical needs of running railways.
Local solar time was replaced because astronomers found it inaccurate.
solution:
The passage traces standard time to railway timetables and safety, and ends: uniform time "began as an operating rule of a transport business": (C).
(D) is out of scope: no scientific objection is mentioned.
(B) overstates one detail: collisions are a risk of mixed local times, not of faulty clocks.
(A) contradicts "finding it inconvenient … gradually followed".

Water hyacinth was carried to many tropical countries as an ornamental plant, admired for its lilac flowers. Freed from the insects that kept it in check in its native range, it spread across lakes and slow rivers, forming mats so dense that boats could not pass and sunlight could not reach the water below. Fish died as oxygen levels fell. Mechanical removal proved costly and temporary, since fragments left behind regrew within months. More lasting success has come from releasing a few species of weevil that feed only on the hyacinth; they do not eradicate it, but they keep it at levels that lakes can tolerate.

According to the passage, which one of the following is TRUE?
options: Mechanical removal permanently cleared most affected lakes.
The weevils released against water hyacinth keep it in check without eliminating it.
Water hyacinth was introduced to block waterways that carried pests.
The released weevils also feed on native water plants.
solution:
"They do not eradicate it, but they keep it at levels that lakes can tolerate": (B).
(C) contradicts "as an ornamental plant".
(A) contradicts "costly and temporary".
(D) contradicts "feed only on the hyacinth".

According to the passage, water hyacinth spread rapidly in its new habitats mainly because

the fish that normally ate it died when oxygen levels fell
its flowers led people to plant it in lake after lake
mechanical removal broke it into fragments that regrew

q:
When a company asked new employees to tick a box if they wished to join its pension scheme, fewer than half did so. When it changed the form so that new employees were enrolled automatically unless they ticked a box to leave, nine in ten stayed in. The scheme, the contribution and the freedom to choose were identical in both cases; only the starting point had moved. Economists who assume that people weigh every option carefully find such results puzzling. Others see them as evidence that many decisions are shaped by inertia, and that whoever designs a form quietly makes choices for those who fill it in.

Which one of the following is best supported by the passage?
options: All economists find the results of the two forms puzzling.
Under automatic enrolment, employees were not allowed to leave the scheme.
The share of employees in the scheme depended on which choice required the employee to take action.
Employees who did not join under the first form did not understand the scheme.
solution:
Under opt-in (action needed to join) fewer than half joined; under opt-out (action needed to leave) nine in ten stayed, with everything else identical: (C).
(B) contradicts "the freedom to choose were identical"; they could tick a box to leave.
(D) is not stated; the passage suggests inertia, not ignorance.
(A) is too strong: only economists "who assume that people weigh every option carefully" are puzzled.

A district survey of rural households reported that 80 percent own at least one mobile phone. Among the phone-owning households, 45 percent said that someone in the household had made a digital payment in the previous month. Officials hailed the figures as proof that digital payments had "reached the majority". A researcher objected that the claim misread the numbers. Households without a phone, she pointed out, had not been asked about digital payments at all, so the survey recorded none for them. She added that a household was counted as a user even if only one member had paid once in the month, so the figures said little about how often payments were actually made.

Based only on the passage, which one of the following can be inferred with certainty?
options: In a majority of phone-owning households, most members made digital payments.
Most phone-owning households made digital payments at least once a week.
The households that reported a digital payment made up less than half of all the households surveyed.
Forty-five percent of all the households surveyed made a digital payment in the previous month.
solution:
Name the bases: 80% of all households own a phone; 45% of those reported a payment; non-owners reported none (they were not asked).
Reporting households $=0.80\times0.45=0.36$ of all, i.e. 36% < 50%: (C).
(D) uses the wrong base (45% is of phone owners, not of all households).
(A) turns a household-level count into a claim about members; one member paying once is enough to count.
(B) is out of scope: the researcher stresses that frequency is unknown.

A health ministry ranked district hospitals by the proportion of admitted patients who died. Several of the best-equipped hospitals, with the most specialists per bed, came near the bottom of the list. A newspaper concluded that the extra specialists were doing more harm than good. The hospitals' doctors pointed out that smaller hospitals routinely transfer their most serious cases to the larger ones, which therefore admit a far higher share of critically ill patients. A fairer comparison, they argued, would look at death rates among patients who arrived in a similar condition.

Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the doctors' response?
options: Specialists at the larger hospitals are paid more than doctors at the smaller ones.
The best-equipped hospitals have more beds than the smaller hospitals.
Smaller hospitals rarely transfer any of their patients to other hospitals.
Among patients admitted in critical condition, fewer die at the best-equipped hospitals than at the smaller ones.
solution:
The doctors say the raw ranking is unfair because the large hospitals receive sicker patients, and that patients in similar condition should be compared. Evidence that, like-for-like, the large hospitals do better supports them: (D).
(B) and (A) are irrelevant to death rates by patient condition.
(C) removes the doctors' own explanation, so it weakens their response.

options: comparing the number of deaths instead of the proportion of patients who died
treating an association as a cause without considering differences in the patients each hospital admits
generalising from a single hospital to every hospital in the country
relying on the opinions of the doctors whose hospitals were ranked
solution:

(C) fails: "several" hospitals were involved and no national claim is made.
(D) fails: the newspaper did not rely on the doctors; the doctors replied to it.
(A) fails: the ranking already used proportions ("the proportion of admitted patients who died").

For years, security guidelines told users to build passwords from a mix of capitals, digits and symbols, and to change them every few months. Studies of real behaviour later found that the rules backfired. Asked to change a password often, people made small, predictable edits, so that "Summer@2023" became "Summer@2024", a pattern attackers soon learned to try. Complex rules also pushed users to write passwords on notes stuck to their screens. Newer guidance therefore favours long passphrases that are easy to remember, changed only when there is evidence of a breach. The lesson, its authors say, is that a rule should be judged by how people actually respond to it, not by how secure it would be if everyone obeyed it perfectly.

Which one of the following best states the lesson drawn in the passage?
options: Passwords should never be changed.
Long passphrases can never be guessed by attackers.
Users who write passwords on notes are careless.
A security rule should be judged by its effect on how people actually behave.
solution:
The last sentence states the lesson: judge a rule "by how people actually respond to it": (D).
(A) is extreme: passwords are to be changed "when there is evidence of a breach".
(B) is extreme and not stated.
(C) is a judgement the passage never makes; it blames the rules, not the users.

q:
For years, security guidelines told users to build passwords from a mix of capitals, digits and symbols, and to change them every few months. Studies of real behaviour later found that the rules backfired. Asked to change a password often, people made small, predictable edits, so that "Summer@2023" became "Summer@2024", a pattern attackers soon learned to try. Complex rules also pushed users to write passwords on notes stuck to their screens. Newer guidance therefore favours long passphrases that are easy to remember, changed only when there is evidence of a breach. The lesson, its authors say, is that a rule should be judged by how people actually respond to it, not by how secure it would be if everyone obeyed it perfectly.

Based only on the passage, which of the following are reasons why the older password rules backfired? (Select all that apply.)
options: Frequent forced changes led people to make predictable edits to their passwords.
Attackers were unable to guess passwords that contained symbols.
Complex rules led people to write their passwords down where others could see them.
The older rules required passphrases too long for people to remember.
solution:
Two reasons are given: predictable edits such as "Summer(D)023" → "Summer(D)024" ((A)) and notes stuck to screens ((C)).
(D) confuses the old rules with the new guidance, which favours long, memorable passphrases.
(B) is not stated and would not explain a failure.

q:
It seems obvious that a more fuel-efficient engine will reduce the fuel a society burns. Yet in the nineteenth century, as steam engines became more efficient, total coal consumption rose rather than fell. The explanation is that efficiency lowered the cost of the work an engine could do, and cheaper work found new uses: factories that could not afford steam power before now installed it. Whether an efficiency gain saves fuel overall thus depends on how strongly demand responds to the lower cost. Where demand is already saturated (few households will light more rooms merely because bulbs are efficient), most of the saving survives; where cheaper energy opens new markets, the saving may be swallowed entirely.

According to the reasoning in the passage, in which one of the following situations is an efficiency gain most likely to reduce total fuel use?
options: A cheaper-to-run engine lets small workshops that had no machines begin to mechanise.
An efficient pump makes it profitable to irrigate land that was earlier left dry.
A more efficient refrigerator is sold in a market where almost every household already owns one and none needs a second.
A more efficient aircraft lowers fares and leads many people to fly for the first time.
solution:
The passage's rule: the saving survives where demand is saturated and is swallowed where cheaper energy opens new uses or markets.
(C) describes saturated demand, so the saving survives.
(A), (D) and (B) each describe cheaper work creating new users (new workshops, first-time flyers, newly irrigated land), the case in which total use may rise.

options: Any improvement in efficiency necessarily lowers total fuel consumption.
Steam engines became more efficient during the nineteenth century.
Demand for household lighting is close to saturation.

solution:
The passage opens with what "seems obvious" (efficiency reduces fuel burnt) and shows it can fail: (A).
(D), (C) and (B) are claims the passage itself accepts and uses in its explanation.

q:
We sometimes imagine that ancient books were lost in great fires. Most were lost more quietly. Texts were written on papyrus or palm leaf, materials that decay within a few generations in a humid climate, so a work survived only if someone thought it worth copying again and again. Each generation of copyists therefore acted as a filter: popular school texts were copied hundreds of times, while technical treatises with few readers were copied rarely, and a single neglected century could end a work's existence. What survives today is less a random sample of ancient writing than a record of what later readers chose to keep.

It can be inferred from the passage that an ancient text that survives today is more likely to have been
options: a work that many later readers thought worth copying
a technical treatise with a small, specialised readership
written on palm leaf rather than on papyrus
a work that was kept far away from any library fire
solution:
Survival depended on repeated copying, and popular texts were copied far more often: (A).
(D) relies on the fire story the passage says explains few losses.
(B) reverses the passage: such treatises "were copied rarely".
(C) makes a comparison the passage never makes; both materials decay.

q:
Food waste buried in a landfill does not simply disappear. Sealed under layers of other rubbish, it breaks down without oxygen, and the bacteria that do this work release methane, a gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide over the following few decades. Composting the same waste in open, regularly turned heaps lets different bacteria break it down with oxygen, producing mostly carbon dioxide and a soil conditioner that farmers can use. Several cities now collect kitchen waste separately for this reason, although residents' willingness to sort their rubbish varies widely from one neighbourhood to another.

According to the passage, why do several cities collect kitchen waste separately?
options: So that the total volume of rubbish sent to landfills is reduced
Because residents in all neighbourhoods prefer to sort their rubbish
So that it can be broken down with oxygen, releasing less methane and yielding a useful product
Because composting removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere
solution:
"For this reason" refers to the contrast just drawn: landfill decay without oxygen releases methane, composting with oxygen gives mostly carbon dioxide plus a soil conditioner: (C).
(A) may be true in reality but is not the reason given.
(B) contradicts "varies widely".
(D) is wrong: composting produces carbon dioxide.

q:
There was a time when leisure was a mark of status, and the wealthy took care to be seen doing nothing in particular. Today the badge of importance is to have no time at all. Ask a successful professional how she is, and she will tell you, with evident satisfaction, that she is "swamped". Calendars are displayed like trophies; a free afternoon is something to be explained, almost apologised for. One may wonder whether all this busyness produces anything more than the impression of it, but to wonder aloud is to risk being thought someone with too little to do.

The tone of the passage is best described as
options: neutral, reporting facts without any judgement
gently ironic about the prestige now attached to being busy
angry and accusatory towards wealthy people
admiring of professionals who work long hours
solution:
Clues: calendars "displayed like trophies", saying "swamped" "with evident satisfaction", a free afternoon "almost apologised for", and the doubt whether busyness produces more than "the impression of it". Mild mockery without hostility: (B).
(D) misses the irony.
(C) is too strong; there is no anger, and the target is a social habit, not the wealthy.
(A) ignores the evaluative wording.

The last sentence of the passage suggests that
options: the author has too little work to do
busy people produce more than people with free time
leisure has regained the prestige it once had
questioning the value of busyness may itself be taken as a sign of low status
solution:
To wonder aloud is "to risk being thought someone with too little to do", and having little to do is now low status: (D).
(B) is what the author doubts.
(A) reads a general remark as a personal confession.
(C) contradicts the whole passage.

q:
Snow that falls on the Antarctic plateau rarely melts. Year after year it is buried by fresh snow and slowly compressed into ice, and in the process tiny bubbles of air are sealed inside. Each bubble is a sample of the atmosphere at the time it was trapped. By drilling cores several kilometres long and measuring the gases in bubbles at different depths, scientists can reconstruct the composition of the air over hundreds of thousands of years. The method has one built-in blur: the snow near the surface stays porous for decades before it closes off, so the air in a bubble is somewhat younger than the ice that surrounds it.

Based only on the passage, which one of the following can be inferred?
options: Ice cores can record the atmosphere for only the last few decades.
Snow on the Antarctic plateau melts every summer.
Bubbles deeper in a core contain younger air than bubbles nearer the surface.
The air in a bubble and the ice around it do not date from exactly the same time.
solution:
The air in a bubble "is somewhat younger than the ice that surrounds it": (D).
(C) reverses depth and age; deeper layers were buried earlier.
(A) contradicts "hundreds of thousands of years".
(B) contradicts "rarely melts".

q:
A city made bus travel free for college students, expecting that many who drove to college would switch to buses and that traffic near the campuses would ease. A year later, bus ridership among students had doubled, yet traffic near the campuses was no lighter. A survey explained why. Most of the new riders had previously walked or cycled to college, while the students who drove continued to drive, valuing the door-to-door convenience of a car far more than the fare they could now save.

Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
options: The bus fare had not been the main reason why students who drove avoided the bus.
The scheme failed to increase bus ridership among students.
Students who drove to college could not afford bus fares.
Traffic near the campuses became heavier after the scheme began.
solution:
Once the fare was removed, drivers still drove, "valuing the door-to-door convenience … far more than the fare": the fare was not what kept them off buses: (A).
(B) contradicts "ridership … had doubled".
(D) overstates "no lighter" (unchanged is not heavier).
(C) is contradicted: the fare was not their concern.

q:
Satellite navigation is usually thought of as a way of finding one's position, but at heart it is a system for distributing time. Each satellite carries atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts the exact moment at which each signal left it. A receiver compares these moments with the times of arrival; since radio signals travel at a known speed, each delay gives a distance, and distances to four or more satellites fix a position. Because a timing error of a single microsecond corresponds to a position error of about three hundred metres, the clocks must be extraordinarily accurate. The same broadcast time is now used, quietly, by power grids and banks to keep their own equipment synchronised.

Based only on the passage, which of the following statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: A clock error of one microsecond leads to a position error of about three kilometres.
Some users of satellite navigation signals rely on them for something other than finding a position.
A receiver needs signals from only one satellite to fix its position.
A receiver works out its distance from a satellite from the time a signal takes to reach it.
solution:
(D): "each delay gives a distance".
(B): power grids and banks use the broadcast time "to keep their own equipment synchronised".
(C) contradicts "four or more satellites".
(A) misreads the figure: about three hundred metres, not three kilometres.

q:
For centuries before steamships, trade across the Indian Ocean ran on a timetable set by the wind. From roughly May to September the monsoon blows from the south-west, carrying ships from Arabia and East Africa toward India; from November to March it reverses, carrying them back. A merchant who missed the turn of the wind might wait months in a foreign port for the next one. These enforced stays had consequences far beyond commerce. Traders married locally, built places of worship and learned one another's languages, and port towns along the ocean's rim came to share foods, words and customs to a degree that would be surprising if one looked only at the distances between them.

Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: The arrival of steamships ended all cultural exchange between the port towns.
The monsoon blows from the south-west for most of the year.
The cultural links among port towns owed much to the time merchants were obliged to spend abroad.
Merchants preferred staying in foreign ports to returning home.
solution:
Missing the wind forced months-long stays; "these enforced stays" led to marriages, places of worship and shared languages, foods and customs: (C).
(D) contradicts "enforced"; nothing is said about preference.
(B) contradicts the timetable: south-west only from roughly May to September, reversing from November.
(A) is extreme and out of scope.

q:
In one experiment, volunteers learned a list of word pairs in the evening and were tested the next morning. Half of them had slept normally; the other half had been kept awake through the night. The volunteers who had slept remembered substantially more pairs. The researchers were careful in their conclusion. Sleep soon after learning, they wrote, appears to help memory, but their study could not show whether the benefit came from sleep itself or simply from the absence, during sleep, of new experiences that might interfere with what had just been learned.

Which one of the following best describes the researchers' conclusion?
options: New experiences after learning always improve memory.
Sleep is the only factor that improves memory.
Sleep after learning seems to help recall, but why it helps is still uncertain.
People remember better if they stay awake after learning.
solution:
They say sleep "appears to help memory" but cannot tell whether the cause is sleep itself or the absence of interfering experiences: (C).
(B) is extreme ("only").
(D) reverses the result.
(A) reverses the suggested mechanism: new experiences might interfere with memory.

q:
A forest department reported that the number of tigers counted in a reserve had risen by 40 percent over four years, and attributed the rise to its stricter anti-poaching patrols. During the same four years, the department had replaced its older method of counting, which relied on identifying individual tigers from their pugmarks (footprints), with camera traps that photograph every animal passing a fixed point and identify individuals by their stripe patterns. Pugmarks vary with the softness of the soil, and the same footprint can look quite different on sand and on clay.

Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the department's explanation for the rise in the tiger count?
options: When both methods were used together in a neighbouring reserve, camera traps identified about 40 percent more tigers than pugmark surveys did.
Camera traps are more expensive to install than pugmark surveys are to conduct.
Tiger numbers fell in a nearby reserve that did not tighten its patrols.
Poaching cases in the reserve fell sharply after the patrols were made stricter.
solution:
The department credits patrols. The passage hints at an alternative cause: the counting method changed. If camera traps alone record about 40% more tigers than pugmarks for the same population, the whole 40% rise could be an artefact of the method: (A).
(D) and (C) support the patrol explanation.
(B) is irrelevant to the size of the count.

q:
Children who begin school in a language they do not speak at home face two tasks at once: learning the language and learning through it. In the early years the first task often swallows the second, and a child who could easily grasp an idea in her own language is marked as slow because she cannot follow the teacher's explanation. Programmes that teach the first years of school in the home language, and introduce the second language gradually, have found that their pupils later do as well in the second language as pupils taught in it from the start, and better in other subjects. The finding challenges a common belief that the earlier and more completely a child is immersed in a new language, the better.

According to the passage, the "common belief" mentioned in the last sentence is challenged because
options: children are unable to learn two languages at the same time
pupils immersed in the second language did better in all other subjects
pupils first taught in their home language never learned the second language well
pupils first taught in their home language later did as well in the second language as pupils immersed from the start
solution:
The belief is that earlier, fuller immersion is better. The programmes found that home-language pupils later matched immersed pupils in the second language (and did better in other subjects), so early immersion gave no advantage: (D).
(C) contradicts the finding.
(A) is an extreme claim the passage never makes.
(B) contradicts the finding ("better in other subjects" refers to the home-language pupils).

q:
During a thunderstorm, the flash of lightning and the sound of thunder are produced at the same moment, but they reach an observer at very different times. Light covers the distance almost instantly, whereas sound travels roughly one kilometre in three seconds. An observer who counts the seconds between the flash and the rumble can therefore estimate how far away the strike was. Safety guidelines use the same principle: if the gap is less than about thirty seconds, the storm is close enough to be dangerous, and people outdoors are advised to seek shelter at once rather than wait for the rain to begin.

An observer counts 15 seconds between a flash of lightning and its thunder. Based only on the passage, which one of the following is correct?
options: The strike was about 5 km away, and the observer need not seek shelter until the rain begins.
The strike was about 15 km away, and the observer need not seek shelter yet.
The strike was about 45 km away, and the observer should seek shelter at once.
The strike was about 5 km away, and the observer should seek shelter at once.
solution:
Sound covers about 1 km in 3 s, so 15 s → $15/3 = 5$ km. The gap (15 s) is under 30 s, so the guideline says seek shelter at once: (D).
(B) treats 1 s as 1 km and ignores the 30-second rule.
(A) gets the distance right but contradicts "rather than wait for the rain to begin".
(C) multiplies by 3 instead of dividing.

q:
A company advertised that its face-recognition system was "99 percent accurate". Researchers testing it found that the figure was an average over a test set in which most faces belonged to young men of one ethnic group. For that group the error rate was well under one percent; for older women from other groups it was several times higher. The overall figure was therefore true but uninformative for anyone who belonged to the groups the test set had largely left out. The researchers did not claim that the system was useless. Their point was that a single accuracy number can hide large differences between the people a system serves.

Which one of the following best expresses the researchers' point?
options: Face-recognition systems should not be used at all.
A single overall accuracy figure can conceal much poorer performance for some groups of people.
Young men are harder for the system to recognise than older women.
The company's claim of 99 percent accuracy was false.
solution:
The last sentence states it: "a single accuracy number can hide large differences": (B).
(D) contradicts "true but uninformative".
(A) contradicts "did not claim that the system was useless".
(C) reverses the groups: errors were lowest for young men.

The overall figure was therefore true but uninformative for anyone who belonged to the groups the test set had largely left out. The researchers did not claim that the system was useless. Their point was that a single accuracy number can hide large differences between the people a system serves.

Based only on the passage, which one of the following can be inferred?
options: Had older women from other groups made up a larger share of the test set, the overall accuracy figure would probably have been lower.
The company chose a lopsided test set in order to mislead its customers.
The researchers recommended that the system be withdrawn from sale.
The system misidentified more than half of the older women from other groups.
solution:
The overall figure is an average weighted by who is in the test set. Raising the share of a group with a several-times-higher error rate pulls the average error up and the accuracy down: (A).
(D) is unsupported: "several times" an error rate of under one percent is a few percent, nowhere near half.
(B) assigns a motive the passage never states.
(C) contradicts "did not claim that the system was useless".

q:
On a village common open to every household, each family decides how many goats to graze. An extra goat brings its owner the full benefit of its milk and meat, while the damage it does to the pasture is shared among all the families. Each family therefore has a reason to add goats even when the pasture is already overgrazed, and the common can be ruined although no single family intended it. Yet field studies have found many villages where commons have been managed well for generations. In these villages the users themselves agreed on limits, watched one another, and imposed small but rising penalties on those who broke the rules.

The field studies mentioned in the passage suggest that
options: families add goats to the common because they wish to damage the pasture
every common pasture is eventually ruined by overgrazing
overuse of a shared resource can be avoided when its users set and enforce their own rules
shared pastures are best managed by an authority from outside the village
solution:
The studies found commons "managed well for generations" where "the users themselves agreed on limits, watched one another" and penalised rule-breakers: (C).
(B) is what the studies refute.
(D) contradicts "the users themselves".
(A) contradicts "no single family intended it".

According to the passage, a family has a reason to add a goat even to an overgrazed common because
options: the penalties for overgrazing are small
the other families have agreed to reduce the number of their goats
goats grazing on a common cost their owners nothing to feed
the family gets all the benefit of the extra goat but bears only part of the damage it causes
solution:
"An extra goat brings its owner the full benefit … while the damage … is shared among all the families": (D).
(C) is not stated.
(A) refers to the well-managed villages, where penalties exist to stop overgrazing; it is not the reason given.
(B) is not stated.

q:
Historians value the accounts of foreign travellers because they describe what local writers took for granted. A visitor notices the price of rice, the shape of the houses and the way people greet one another, details a local chronicler would never think worth recording. But the same distance that sharpens a traveller's eye also limits it. He usually stays only a few weeks, speaks the language poorly, and depends on interpreters and hosts who choose what he sees and hears. A careful historian therefore trusts a traveller most on what he could observe for himself and least on what he could only have been told.

According to the passage, a careful historian would place the most trust in which one of the following statements by a foreign traveller?
options: The people of the region had always resented rule by the northern dynasty.
The town had been founded three centuries earlier by a family of merchants.
Most houses on the market street were built of brick and had flat roofs.
The king had secretly poisoned his elder brother to gain the throne.
solution:
Rule: trust the traveller most on "what he could observe for himself". House materials and roofs are visible during a short stay: (C).
(D) (a secret palace crime), (A) (attitudes held over generations) and (B) (events three centuries old) could only have been told to him, through interpreters and hosts, so they deserve the least trust.

q:
As Himalayan glaciers retreat, meltwater collects behind the loose ridges of rock and debris that the glaciers once pushed ahead of them. These ridges, called moraines, were never shaped to hold back water. A lake that grows behind one can break through it suddenly, after an earthquake, a heavy rainstorm, or an ice avalanche that sends a wave over the top, releasing within hours a flood that may sweep away villages and bridges far downstream. Some lakes are being lowered deliberately by cutting channels or siphoning water out. Such work is expensive and difficult at high altitude, so authorities must decide which of hundreds of lakes to treat first.

Based only on the passage, which of the following can be inferred? (Select all that apply.)
options: Lowering the water level of glacial lakes is cheap and easy work.
A moraine lake can break through its ridge even in the absence of heavy rain.
Moraines were built by people to store meltwater.
The danger from a moraine lake can reach places far from the lake itself.
solution:
(D): the flood "may sweep away villages and bridges far downstream".
(B): an earthquake or an ice avalanche can also trigger a breach.
(A) contradicts "expensive and difficult at high altitude".
(C) contradicts the passage: glaciers pushed the debris; the ridges "were never shaped to hold back water".

q:
Ask a single person to guess the number of beans in a jar and the answer may be far off. Ask several hundred people independently and the average of their guesses is often remarkably close to the true number, because individual errors in both directions tend to cancel out. The effect depends critically on independence. If the guessers can hear one another, early and confident guesses pull later ones toward them, the errors begin to point the same way, and the average loses much of its accuracy. A crowd, in other words, is wise only when its members are not listening to each other.

According to the passage, which one of the following procedures is most likely to give an accurate average estimate?
options: A small group adopts the guess of its most confident member.
A large group discusses the question together and then each member writes down a guess.
Each member of a large group announces a guess aloud, one after another.
Each member of a large group writes down a guess privately before any guess is revealed.
solution:
Accuracy needs a large number of independent guesses, so that errors cancel: (D).
(B) and (C) let members hear one another, so early guesses pull later ones and errors line up.
(A) replaces many guesses with one.

q:
When a crop is engineered to produce its own insecticide, the pests that feed on it face strong pressure to evolve resistance. Any rare insect that happens to carry a resistance gene survives and breeds, while its neighbours die. To slow this, farmers are advised to plant a "refuge" of the ordinary crop beside the engineered one. Insects in the refuge are not exposed to the toxin, so susceptible insects survive there in large numbers. When the rare resistant survivors from the engineered field mate, they are far more likely to mate with these susceptible insects than with each other, and since resistance in many pests appears only when both parents pass on the gene, most of their offspring remain vulnerable.

The refuge strategy described in the passage depends on which one of the following?
options: Insects in the refuge are killed by the toxin in the engineered crop.
Insects from the refuge and insects from the engineered field mix and mate with one another.
Resistance appears in an insect whenever either of its parents carries the gene.
The refuge is planted with a crop different from the engineered one.
solution:
The point of the refuge is that rare resistant survivors mate mostly with susceptible refuge insects. That works only if the two populations meet and mate: (B). Negate it and the refuge has no effect on the resistant insects' offspring.
(A) contradicts "not exposed to the toxin".
(C) contradicts "only when both parents pass on the gene", and would defeat the strategy.
(D) contradicts "a refuge of the ordinary crop".

q:

Based only on the passage, the refuge strategy would be LEAST effective against a pest in which
options: resistance appears in the offspring even when only one parent passes on the gene
adult insects fly freely between neighbouring fields
the resistance gene is extremely rare at the start
very large numbers of susceptible insects live in the refuge
solution:
The strategy works because a resistant × susceptible mating gives mostly vulnerable offspring, which holds only when resistance needs the gene from both parents. If one copy is enough, those matings produce resistant offspring and the refuge no longer dilutes resistance: (A).
(B) helps the strategy (it brings the two populations together).
(C) helps (resistant survivors are few, so they rarely meet each other).
(D) helps (more susceptible mates).

q:
Two passengers sitting side by side on the same flight may have paid very different fares. The airline is not being careless. A seat on a particular flight cannot be stored once the plane has left, so the airline tries to sell each seat for as much as some customer will pay. Business travellers, who often book late and cannot change their dates, are charged more; holiday-makers, who book months ahead and could easily choose another airline or another week, are offered lower fares to win them over. As the departure date approaches and unsold seats remain, prices may even fall again.

According to the passage, holiday-makers are offered lower fares mainly because
options: the airline makes a loss on business travellers
they are usually given seats at the back of the aircraft
they can more easily switch to another airline or another date
seats booked early cost the airline less to provide
solution:
Holiday-makers "could easily choose another airline or another week" and are offered lower fares "to win them over": (C).
(B), (A) and (D) are not stated anywhere in the passage.

q:
Once a technical standard is widely adopted, it can outlive the reasons for choosing it. Each new user picks the standard because everyone else already uses it: spare parts are cheaper, skilled workers are easier to find, and equipment works together. A rival design may be better in every technical respect and still fail, because the first users to switch would bear all the costs of incompatibility, while the benefits would arrive only after many others had switched too. For this reason, changes of standard usually happen only when some outside event, such as a new government rule or the collapse of the old industry, forces many users to move at once.

According to the passage, why may a technically superior rival standard fail?
options: Technically superior designs are always more expensive to manufacture.
Its first users would bear the costs of incompatibility before enough others switched to bring the benefits.
Governments usually forbid the adoption of new standards.
Users are generally unaware that better designs exist.
solution:
The third sentence: the first switchers "would bear all the costs of incompatibility, while the benefits would arrive only after many others had switched too": (B).
(A) is an extreme claim not made.
(C) reverses the passage: a government rule is named as something that can force a change.
(D) is not stated.

For this reason, changes of standard usually happen only when some outside event, such as a new government rule or the collapse of the old industry, forces many users to move at once.

According to the passage, a change of standard is most likely to happen when
options: spare parts for the existing standard become cheaper
a few users decide to switch early
a rival design becomes slightly better in technical terms
an outside event compels many users to switch at the same time
solution:
"Changes of standard usually happen only when some outside event … forces many users to move at once": (D).
(C): even a design better "in every technical respect" may fail.
(B): early switchers bear the costs and do not trigger a change on their own.
(A) would strengthen the existing standard.

q:
In a trial of a new drug, 2,000 adults at risk of a certain heart condition were divided at random into two equal groups. One group took the drug for five years and the other took a dummy pill. By the end of the trial, 20 people in the dummy group and 10 in the drug group had developed the condition. The drug's maker announced that the drug "halves the risk". A commentator offered a second way of stating the same result: of every 100 people who take the drug for five years, about one is spared the condition who would otherwise have developed it.

Based only on the passage, which one of the following is correct?
options: The commentator's statement agrees with the trial results, but the maker's does not.
Both the maker's statement and the commentator's statement agree with the trial results.
Neither statement agrees with the trial results.
The maker's statement agrees with the trial results, but the commentator's does not.
solution:
Each group has 1,000 people. Risk without the drug $=20/1000=2\%$; with the drug $=10/1000=1\%$.
Maker: 1% is half of 2% (relative reduction) ✔.
Commentator: $2\%-1\%=1\%$, i.e. about 1 in 100 spared (absolute reduction) ✔. So (B).
Trap: thinking that "halves the risk" and "1 in 100" contradict each other; they describe the same result relative to different bases.

A commentator offered a second way of stating the same result: of every 100 people who take the drug for five years, about one is spared the condition who would otherwise have developed it.

Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Ten people in the drug group were cured of the condition by the drug.
The drug prevents the condition in half of all the people who take it.
About 98 of every 100 people in the dummy group did not develop the condition during the trial.
Without the drug, half of the people at risk would develop the condition.
solution:
Dummy group: 1,000 people, 20 developed the condition, so 980 did not, i.e. 98 per 100: (C).
(B) misreads "halves the risk" as protecting half the people; only 1 in 100 is spared.
(D) confuses the 2% risk with 50%.
(A) misreads the data: 10 people in the drug group developed the condition.

q:
Engineers often protect a critical function by duplicating it: two pumps instead of one, so that if one fails the other takes over. The arithmetic is encouraging. If each pump fails on one day in a thousand, and the failures are independent, both will fail on the same day only about once in a million days. But the arithmetic depends entirely on that word "independent". Two pumps fed by the same power line, installed by the same crew, or sitting in the same basement that floods will tend to fail together, and the true chance of losing both may be closer to that of losing one. Good design therefore duplicates not only the component but also separates whatever could make the copies fail together: separate power, separate locations, sometimes different manufacturers.

At a plant with two duplicate pumps, which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the estimate that both pumps fail on the same day only about once in a million days?
options: Both pumps draw power from a single cable that is sometimes cut during maintenance work.
The two pumps were made by different manufacturers.
The two pumps are housed in separate buildings on opposite sides of the plant.
Each pump, taken alone, fails on about one day in a thousand.
solution:
The million-to-one figure assumes independent failures. A shared power cable is a common cause that knocks out both pumps at once: (A).
(B) and (C) are exactly the separations the passage recommends; they support independence.
(D) is the input the estimate already uses.

q:
A city introduced a charge of ₹5 on every plastic carry bag handed out by shops. Within a year, the number of carry bags supplied by shops had fallen by about four-fifths, and officials declared that the charge had greatly reduced the plastic waste thrown away by households. An environmental group was less sure. Many households, it noted, had earlier reused shop bags to line their dustbins; with free bags gone, they were now buying packs of bin liners, which are also made of plastic and are often thicker.

The officials' conclusion assumes that
options: shops in the city have stopped selling bin liners
₹5 is a large sum for most households in the city
most households now carry their own cloth bags when they go shopping
the fall in carry bags was not largely offset by other plastic items bought for the same purposes
solution:
Evidence: fewer shop bags. Conclusion: much less household plastic waste. The gap: households must not have replaced the bags with other plastic. Negate (D) (substitutes offset the fall) and the conclusion fails; this is exactly the environmental group's worry.
(C) is not needed; households could manage with fewer bags in many ways.
(B) is not needed; the fall in bags is already observed.
(A) is not needed and is irrelevant to the officials' reasoning.

q:
A city introduced a charge of ₹5 on every plastic carry bag handed out by shops. Within a year, the number of carry bags supplied by shops had fallen by about four-fifths, and officials declared that the charge had greatly reduced the plastic waste thrown away by households. An environmental group was less sure. Many households, it noted, had earlier reused shop bags to line their dustbins; with free bags gone, they were now buying packs of bin liners, which are also made of plastic and are often thicker.

If accurate, the environmental group's observation shows that
options: the fall in the number of carry bags may overstate the fall in households' plastic waste
households have stopped using dustbins
bin liners are cheaper than carry bags
the charge has increased the plastic waste thrown away by households
solution:
Some of the plastic once carried home as shop bags now arrives as bought bin liners, so the four-fifths fall in bags need not mean a similar fall in waste: (A).
(D) is too strong: the passage gives no figures showing waste rose.
(C) is not stated.
(B) contradicts the observation: they now buy liners for their dustbins.

q:
Early modern mapmakers disliked empty space. Where they had no information about the interior of a continent, they often filled it with plausible-looking mountains, rivers and towns, copied from older maps or taken from the report of a single traveller. Some of these features survived for centuries, faithfully reproduced by later mapmakers who assumed that their predecessors had good reasons for drawing them. A change came when some mapmakers began to leave unknown regions blank. The blank spaces were less pleasing to the eye, but they were honest, and they told explorers exactly where knowledge ended, which is, after all, where exploration begins.

According to the passage, the main merit of leaving unknown regions blank was that
options: it removed every error from the maps
it made maps cheaper to produce
it showed clearly where reliable knowledge ended
it made the maps more attractive to look at
solution:
Blank spaces "were honest, and they told explorers exactly where knowledge ended": (C).
(D) contradicts "less pleasing to the eye".
(B) is out of scope.
(A) is extreme: leaving the interior blank does not correct other errors.

Which one of the following can be inferred about the invented features described in the passage?
options: They were deliberately invented to mislead rival explorers.
All of them were taken from the report of a single traveller.
They were removed as soon as the first traveller reached the interior.
They lasted partly because later mapmakers trusted the maps of their predecessors.
solution:
Features "survived for centuries, faithfully reproduced by later mapmakers who assumed that their predecessors had good reasons": (D).
(A) assigns a motive; the passage says mapmakers "disliked empty space".
(C) contradicts "survived for centuries".
(B) is too strong: they were copied from older maps or taken from a traveller.

q:
In several farming regions, electricity for irrigation pumps is supplied free or for a flat monthly fee, regardless of how much is used. The policy was meant to help small farmers, and it did lower their costs. But because pumping for an extra hour costs a farmer nothing, wells run longer than the crops need, and water tables in some districts have fallen by more than a metre a year. As the water sinks, farmers must buy more powerful pumps and drill deeper wells, an expense that falls hardest on the small farmers the policy was meant to protect. Some states are now experimenting with paying farmers for the electricity they do not use, keeping their income support while restoring a reason to save water.

Based only on the passage, which of the following statements are supported? (Select all that apply.)
options: The free-electricity policy reduced the cost of pumping for farmers.
The falling water table has brought new costs to small farmers.
The experimental scheme withdraws all income support from farmers.
Under the experimental scheme, a farmer who uses less electricity is better off financially.
solution:
(A): the policy "did lower their costs".
(B): deeper wells and stronger pumps are an expense "that falls hardest on the small farmers".
(D): farmers are paid "for the electricity they do not use", so using less earns more.
(C) contradicts "keeping their income support".

q:
A fitness chain surveyed its members and found that those who had belonged for more than five years were, on average, much fitter than those who had joined in the past year. Its advertisements now claim that "five years with us will transform your fitness". A statistician pointed out that the members who stay for five years are not a random sample of those who join. People who find exercise hard or unrewarding tend to quit within months, so long-standing members may have been fitter, or more committed to exercise, from the very start.

The statistician's criticism is that the advertisement
options: is based on a survey of too few members to be reliable
assumes that regular exercise cannot improve fitness
ignores the possibility that long-standing members differ from new members for reasons other than their years of membership
compares the fitness of members with that of people who never joined
solution:
Those who stay five years are a self-selected group (the less fit or less committed quit early), so their fitness may predate their membership: (C).
(A): sample size is never questioned.
(D): the survey compares two groups of members, not members with non-members.
(B) is the opposite of what the advertisement assumes.

q:
A fitness chain surveyed its members and found that those who had belonged for more than five years were, on average, much fitter than those who had joined in the past year. Its advertisements now claim that "five years with us will transform your fitness". A statistician pointed out that the members who stay for five years are not a random sample of those who join. People who find exercise hard or unrewarding tend to quit within months, so long-standing members may have been fitter, or more committed to exercise, from the very start.

Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the advertisement's claim against the statistician's criticism?
options: Members who have belonged for more than five years are, on average, younger than recent joiners.
The fitness chain has opened many new branches over the past five years.
Members who quit within a few months were, on joining, less fit than those who stayed.
Among members who stayed five years, fitness measured on joining and again after five years had improved greatly for nearly all.
solution:
The criticism is that long-standing members may have started fitter. Measuring the same people at joining and five years later removes the selection problem and shows real change: (D).
(C) supports the statistician: those who stayed were fitter from the start.
(B) is irrelevant.
(A) offers another alternative explanation (age), weakening the claim.

q:
When enough people in a community are immune to an infection, a single case can no longer start a large outbreak, because the infected person meets too few people who can catch the disease. This protects even those who are not immune themselves, such as newborn babies too young to be vaccinated. The proportion of immune people needed depends on how contagious the disease is: the more people a single case would infect in a population where nobody is immune, the higher that proportion must be. For a highly contagious disease, the required level of immunity can exceed nine in ten.

Based only on the passage, which one of the following is TRUE?
options: A less contagious disease needs a smaller proportion of immune people to prevent large outbreaks.
In a community with enough immune people, not even a single case of the disease can occur.
Newborn babies are protected only if they are vaccinated.
Every disease needs more than nine in ten people to be immune to prevent large outbreaks.
solution:
"The more people a single case would infect …, the higher that proportion must be", so a less contagious disease needs a smaller proportion: (A).
(C) contradicts the passage: community immunity protects babies "too young to be vaccinated".
(D) overgeneralises: over nine in ten is for "a highly contagious disease".
(B) misreads the passage: a single case can occur; it just cannot start a large outbreak.

q:
Why do employers pay graduates more? One answer is that a degree teaches skills that make a worker more productive. Another is that the degree mainly signals qualities the worker already had: the persistence to finish a long course and the ability that won her admission in the first place. The two answers predict different things. If degrees mainly teach skills, a student who completes three years of a four-year course should earn about three-quarters of the extra pay that graduates receive. If degrees mainly signal, the same student should earn little of it, because what employers reward is completion.

According to the passage, which one of the following observations would favour the signalling answer over the skills answer?
options: Graduates earn more than people without degrees.
Students who leave in the final year of a four-year course earn barely more than people who never enrolled.
Students who leave after three years of a four-year course earn about three-quarters of the graduates' extra pay.
Graduates of every university earn more than non-graduates.
solution:
Signalling predicts that a student who completes three of four years earns "little" of the premium, because only completion is rewarded: (B) matches this.
(C) is what the skills answer predicts.
(A) and (D) are predicted by both answers, so they cannot decide between them.

q:
Reef-building corals live in partnership with tiny algae that dwell inside their tissues. The algae supply most of the coral's food through photosynthesis and give it its colour; the coral offers them shelter and nutrients. When the sea stays unusually warm for several weeks, the partnership breaks down and the coral expels the algae, turning white. A bleached coral is not dead. If temperatures return to normal soon enough, algae can recolonise it; if the heat lasts too long, the coral starves. Because warm spells are becoming longer and more frequent, many reefs now face bleaching again before they have recovered from the last episode.

According to the passage, why can a long-lasting warm spell kill a bleached coral?
options: Because white corals are eaten by fish
Because warm water dissolves the coral's skeleton
Because the coral has lost the algae that supply most of its food
Because the algae begin to feed on the coral
solution:
The algae "supply most of the coral's food"; a bleached coral has expelled them, and "if the heat lasts too long, the coral starves": (C).
(B), (D) and (A) are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.

q:
For periods before mass schooling, historians often estimate literacy from marriage registers, counting the share of brides and grooms who signed their names rather than making a mark. The method is attractive because registers survive in large numbers and cover all classes of society. Its weakness is that signing is not the same as reading. In many places reading was taught before writing, and children who left school early might read fluently yet never learn to write even their names. Conversely, a few people learned to sign their names and nothing else. Most historians conclude that signature rates are a reasonable guide to how literacy changed over time, but a doubtful guide to its actual level in any single year.

According to the passage, why may signature rates understate the number of people who could read?
options: Some people who could read had never learned to write their names.
Marriage registers recorded only the upper classes.
Many marriage registers from the period have been lost.
A few people who signed their names could not read anything else.
solution:
Readers who never learned to write their names made a mark and were counted as illiterate, so the count of readers is too low: (A).
(C) contradicts "registers survive in large numbers".
(D) is true in the passage but works the other way: it makes signature rates overstate literacy.
(B) contradicts "cover all classes of society".

For periods before mass schooling, historians often estimate literacy from marriage registers, counting the share of brides and grooms who signed their names rather than making a mark. The method is attractive because registers survive in large numbers and cover all classes of society. Its weakness is that signing is not the same as reading. In many places reading was taught before writing, and children who left school early might read fluently yet never learn to write even their names. Conversely, a few people learned to sign their names and nothing else. Most historians conclude that signature rates are a reasonable guide to how literacy changed over time, but a doubtful guide to its actual level in any single year.

The historians' conclusion that signature rates are a reasonable guide to changes in literacy over time assumes that
options: literacy rose steadily in every region over the period
everyone who could read was also able to sign his or her name
marriage registers are more reliable than school records
the gap between being able to sign and being able to read did not change sharply over the period studied
solution:
A biased measure can still track trends if its bias is roughly constant. If the sign-versus-read gap itself shifted (say, writing began to be taught earlier), signature rates could rise without any rise in reading. Negating (D) breaks the conclusion, so it is the assumption.
(B) contradicts the passage (some readers could not sign).
(C): school records are never mentioned.
(A) is a possible finding, not a premise of the method.

q:
Software teams under deadline pressure often take shortcuts: a quick patch instead of a proper redesign, a copied block of code instead of a shared function. Each shortcut saves time today, but it makes the next change slightly harder, because the next programmer must understand it and work around it. Engineers call the accumulated cost "technical debt", and the metaphor is apt in one further respect. Like financial debt, it is not always a mistake to take it on; a young company that would otherwise miss its launch may be right to borrow. The danger lies in forgetting that the debt exists, for then the interest, the extra effort on every future change, goes on being paid without anyone having decided to pay it.

In the passage, the "interest" on technical debt refers to
options: the money a young company borrows in order to meet its launch date
the extra effort that every later change requires because of earlier shortcuts
the time a team saves by taking a shortcut
the programmers' eagerness to redesign the code properly
solution:
The passage defines it: "the interest, the extra effort on every future change": (B).
(A) reads the metaphor literally as financial borrowing.
(C) reverses it: the time saved is the "loan", not the interest.
(D) puns on another sense of "interest".

q:
