The danger lies in forgetting that the debt exists, for then the interest, the extra effort on every future change, goes on being paid without anyone having decided to pay it.

Which one of the following best expresses the author's view of shortcuts in software development?
options: They are harmless provided programmers do not think about them.
They should be avoided in all circumstances.
They can be justified, but their continuing cost should be recognised and kept in view.
They cost nothing as long as the software is launched on time.
solution:
"It is not always a mistake to take it on" (justifiable), but "the danger lies in forgetting that the debt exists" (cost must be tracked): (C).
(B) contradicts the young-company example.
(D) contradicts "makes the next change slightly harder".
(A) reverses the danger: forgetting is the problem.

q:
Earthworms are often praised as friends of the soil, and in farmland they usually are: their burrows let in air and water, and their casts mix organic matter into the ground. But in some northern forests that had no earthworms from the end of the last ice age until recent times, worms introduced by people, often anglers discarding bait, are changing the forest floor. The thick layer of fallen leaves on which native seedlings depend is eaten away within a few years, and certain wildflowers have become scarce where the worms have spread. Whether an organism is beneficial, it seems, depends less on the organism than on where it is.

Which one of the following can NOT be inferred from the passage?
options: Earthworms harm the soil in most farmland.
The spread of earthworms can change which plants grow in a forest.
Some earthworms in northern forests got there through human activity.
Some northern forests had no earthworms for a long period before recent times.
solution:
(A) contradicts "in farmland they usually are" friends of the soil, so it cannot be inferred.
(D): no earthworms "from the end of the last ice age until recent times".
(B): "certain wildflowers have become scarce where the worms have spread".
(C): "worms introduced by people, often anglers discarding bait".

q:
"Only members can borrow books from the club library." Ravi borrowed a book from the club library last week.
Based only on the above, which one of the following can be logically inferred?
options: Non-members are allowed to read books inside the club library.
Ravi is a member of the club.
Every member of the club borrowed a book last week.
Ravi borrows a book from the club library every week.
solution:
"Only members can borrow" means: borrowed ⇒ member. Ravi borrowed, so he is a member: (B).
(C) reverses the rule (member ⇒ borrowed) and over-generalises.
(D) turns one borrowing into a habit.
(A) is out of scope; the rule says nothing about reading inside.

q:
Statement: If it rains on Saturday, the match will be postponed. The match was not postponed.
Conclusions:
I. It did not rain on Saturday.
II. The match was played on Saturday.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
Rule: rain ⇒ postponed. Not postponed ⇒ not rain (contrapositive), so I follows.
II does not follow: "not postponed" does not mean "played"; the match could have been cancelled for some other reason.
Answer: (A).

q:
Statement: If the power supply fails, the factory stops production. The factory stopped production on Monday.
Conclusions:
I. The power supply failed on Monday.
II. The power supply did not fail on Monday.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
Rule: power failure ⇒ production stops. Knowing that production stopped does not tell us why: it may have stopped for another reason (a holiday, a strike). So I (affirming the consequent) does not follow.
II does not follow either: a power failure on Monday is entirely possible.
Answer: (D).
Trap: reading "if" as "if and only if".

q:
"Unless an application form is signed, it will not be processed." Meera's application form was processed.
Which one of the following can be logically inferred?
options: Meera's application form was signed.
Meera's application form was processed quickly.
Every signed application form is processed.
Meera signed the form in front of an official.
solution:
"Unless S, not P" = "if not S then not P" = "P ⇒ S". The form was processed, so it was signed: (A).
(C) is the converse (signed ⇒ processed), which the rule does not give.
(D) adds details (who signed, where) not stated.
(B): nothing is said about speed.

q:
In a college, 70% of the students play cricket and 60% play football.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Exactly 30% of the students play both games.
At least 30% of the students play both games.
At most 30% of the students play both games.
At least 40% of the students play neither game.
solution:
Both $\ge 70+60-100 = 30\%$, and both $\le 60\%$. So "at least 30%" is certain: (B).
(A) and (C) fail: the overlap can be anywhere from 30% to 60%.
(D) fails: neither $= 100 - (70+60-\text{both})$ is at most 30%, never 40%.

q:
Statement: Every engineer in the firm knows Python. Some people in the firm who know Python also know Java. No one who knows Java works in the accounts section.
Conclusions:
I. Some engineers in the firm know Java.
II. No engineer in the firm works in the accounts section.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
I: the Python-knowers who know Java might all be non-engineers, so I is not certain.
II: only Java-knowers are barred from accounts. An engineer who knows Python but not Java may well work in accounts, so II is not certain.
Answer: (D).
Trap: chaining "some" through "all" in the wrong direction.

q:
Notice in an apartment complex: "Residents are requested to use the stairs instead of the lift between 9 a.m. and 11 a.m. in order to save electricity."
Which one of the following is an assumption implicit in the notice?
options: The lift is out of order between 9 a.m. and 11 a.m.
Electricity costs less after 11 a.m.
All the residents are physically fit.
Running the lift uses electricity.
solution:
Using the stairs can save electricity only if the lift consumes electricity: (D). Negate it and the request makes no sense.
(C) is too strong; the notice is only a request.
(A) contradicts the notice (if it were out of order, no request would be needed).
(B) is not needed: the aim is to use less, not to shift the time of use.

q:
Umbrella sales in a town were 50% higher this July than last July. A shopkeeper concludes that this July was much rainier than last July.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the shopkeeper's conclusion?
options: Last July, the town received less rain than it usually does.
A large factory outlet opened in the town this year and sells umbrellas at half the usual price.
Sales of raincoats in the town were also much higher this July.
Most umbrellas in the town are bought during the rainy season.
solution:
To weaken "more sales ⇒ more rain", give another cause for the extra sales. Halved prices could explain the rise without any extra rain: (B).
(C) is another symptom of more rain, so it strengthens.
(D) is background that fits the conclusion.
(A) makes last July dry, which helps the comparison rather than weakening it.

q:
Students who attend a school's optional evening classes score higher in the final examination than those who do not. The principal concludes that the evening classes improve examination scores.
Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the principal's conclusion?
options: In a trial where students were assigned at random to attend or not attend, those assigned to attend scored higher.
Students with high scores in the previous year are more likely to attend the evening classes.
The evening classes are held in the school library.
Students who attend the evening classes also spend more hours studying at home.
solution:
The rival explanation is self-selection: stronger or more diligent students choose to attend. Random assignment removes that, so a higher score then points to the classes: (A).
(D) and (B) give alternative explanations, so they weaken.
(C) is irrelevant.

q:
"Had the train been on time, Priya would have reached the interview."
Based only on this sentence, which one of the following can be inferred?
options: The train was on time, but Priya missed the interview.
The train was late, and Priya did not reach the interview.
Priya did not wish to attend the interview.
Priya reached the interview, but late.
solution:
"Had X been…, Y would have…" (third conditional) describes an unreal past: in fact X did not happen and Y did not happen. So the train was late and she did not reach: (B).
(A) contradicts "had the train been on time".
(D) contradicts the implied non-arrival.
(C) is out of scope.

q:
Every shop in the market that sells sweets also sells snacks. Shop X, which is in the market, does not sell snacks.
Which one of the following follows logically?
options: No shop in the market sells snacks.
Shop X sells nothing at all.
Shop X sells only sweets.
Shop X does not sell sweets.
solution:
Sells sweets ⇒ sells snacks. Contrapositive: no snacks ⇒ no sweets: (D).
(C) contradicts this.
(A) is an over-generalisation from one shop.
(B) is too strong; X may sell other goods.

q:
Statement: The number of students who passed the examination this year is higher than last year.
Conclusions:
I. The pass percentage this year is higher than last year.
II. More students appeared for the examination this year than last year.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
A higher number of passes can come with a higher, equal or lower percentage, depending on how many appeared, so I does not follow.
II does not follow either: the same or even fewer candidates could have produced more passes if the pass rate rose.
Answer: (D).

q:
Each of the 200 employees of a firm opted for at least one of two plans: 120 opted for the health plan and 90 opted for the pension plan.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Fewer than 100 employees opted for only the health plan.
Exactly 10 employees opted for both plans.
Exactly 30 employees opted for both plans.
Exactly 110 employees opted for only the pension plan.
solution:
Since every employee chose at least one plan, both $=120+90-200=10$ exactly: (B).
(C) subtracts 90 from 120, which is meaningless here.
Only pension $=90-10=80$, so (D) is false.
Only health $=120-10=110$, so (A) is false.

q:
"No student who failed the test was given a scholarship. Some students who were given a scholarship play chess."
Based only on these statements, which of the following must be true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Some students who play chess did not fail the test.
Some students who play chess were given a scholarship.
No student who plays chess failed the test.
Every student who did not fail the test was given a scholarship.
solution:
Take the students who have a scholarship and play chess (there is at least one). They did not fail (scholarship ⇒ not failed). So (A) holds, and "some scholarship holders play chess" converts to (B).
(C) is too strong: other chess players may have failed.
(D) reverses the first statement: not failing is necessary for a scholarship, not sufficient.

q:
"I would have lent you my bicycle if you had asked me," Arjun told Kiran.
Based only on this statement, which one of the following can be inferred?
options: Kiran asked Arjun, but Arjun refused to lend the bicycle.
Arjun lent his bicycle to someone else.
Arjun does not own a bicycle.
Kiran did not ask Arjun for the bicycle.
solution:
"Would have … if you had asked" is an unreal past condition: Kiran did not ask: (D).
(C) contradicts "my bicycle".
(A) contradicts the implied fact that Kiran did not ask.
(B) is out of scope.

q:
"The city will supply water every day only if the reservoir level is above 60%." The city is supplying water every day.
Which one of the following can be logically inferred?
options: The reservoir is completely full.
The reservoir level is above 60%.
Whenever the reservoir level is above 60%, the city supplies water every day.
The city will supply water every day throughout the year.
solution:
"A only if B" means A ⇒ B. Daily supply is happening, so the level is above 60%: (B).
(C) is the converse (B ⇒ A), which "only if" does not give.
(A) is too strong; above 60% need not be full.
(D) extends a present fact into the future.

q:
"A student will receive the gold medal only if she scores above 90 in the final examination." Asha scored 95 in the final examination.
Based only on this information, which one of the following is correct?
options: Asha will receive the gold medal.
Asha will not receive the gold medal.
It cannot be determined whether Asha will receive the gold medal.
Every student who scores above 90 receives the gold medal.
solution:
"Medal only if score > 90" means medal ⇒ score > 90. A score above 90 is necessary, not sufficient, so Asha's 95 does not settle the matter: (C).
(A) treats "only if" as "if".
(B) has no basis; she meets the necessary condition.
(D) is the converse of the rule.

q:
"Every great novelist reads widely. Sunil reads widely. Therefore Sunil will become a great novelist."
Which one of the following arguments has the same logical flaw?
options: Some birds cannot fly. This animal cannot fly. Therefore it may be a bird.
All birds lay eggs. This animal lays eggs. Therefore it is a bird.
No fish can fly. This animal can fly. Therefore it is not a fish.
All birds lay eggs. This animal is a bird. Therefore it lays eggs.
solution:
The original has the form "All A are B; x is B; so x is A" (affirming the consequent): reading widely is necessary for a great novelist, not sufficient. (B) has exactly this form.
(D) is valid (All A are B; x is A; so x is B).
(C) is valid (contrapositive).
(A) claims only a possibility, which is not the flawed certainty of the original.

q:
Since speed cameras were installed on a highway a year ago, accidents on it have fallen by 30%. The traffic department concludes that the cameras reduced accidents.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the department's conclusion?
options: Drivers report slowing down when they approach the cameras.
Accidents rose during the year on nearby roads without cameras.
The cameras were expensive to buy and install.
During the same year, a new expressway opened that took away about a third of the highway's traffic.
solution:
An alternative cause: a third less traffic could by itself cut accidents by about 30%: (D).
(B) strengthens (roads without cameras did worse).
(A) supports the mechanism by which cameras would work.
(C) is irrelevant to whether accidents fell because of the cameras.

q:
Notice: "The public library will remain closed this Sunday for its annual stock-taking."
Which one of the following is an assumption implicit in the notice?
options: The library is ordinarily open on Sundays.
Stock-taking is done every Sunday.
The library has lost many of its books.
Readers prefer to visit the library on Sundays.
solution:
Announcing a special closure on Sunday makes sense only if the library would otherwise be open then: (A).
(B) contradicts "annual".
(C) is not implied; stock-taking is routine.
(D) is not needed for the notice.

q:
In a town, 40% of the households own a car. Of the households that own a car, 25% also own a two-wheeler. Of the households that do not own a car, 50% own a two-wheeler.
Based only on this information, which one of the following is correct?
options: More households own both a car and a two-wheeler than own neither.
Fewer than half of all households own a two-wheeler.
37.5% of all households own a two-wheeler.
Most households that own a two-wheeler also own a car.
solution:
Take 100 households: 40 own a car, of whom $0.25\times40=10$ own a two-wheeler; 60 have no car, of whom $0.5\times60=30$ own one. Two-wheeler owners $=40$ < 50: (B).
(D): only 10 of 40 two-wheeler owners have a car.
(C) averages 25% and 50% without weighting.
(A): both = 10, neither = 30, so it is false.

q:
"The government should build cycle lanes on the city's main roads, because more people would then cycle to work, and traffic jams would ease."
Which one of the following is an assumption on which this argument depends?
options: Every resident of the city owns a bicycle.
Traffic jams in the city are caused only by cars.
Cycle lanes are cheaper to build than new roads.
Some people who now travel to work by motor vehicle would cycle if such lanes existed.
solution:
Jams ease only if the new cyclists come out of motor vehicles; if all new cyclists were former walkers, traffic would not change. Negating (D) breaks the argument.
(A) and (B) are far stronger than needed.
(C) is about cost, which the argument does not discuss.

q:
Statement: The review meeting will be held either on Monday or online. The meeting was not held online.
Conclusions:
I. The meeting was held on Monday.
II. The meeting was not held at all.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
"Either A or B" with B false leaves A: the meeting was held on Monday, so I follows.
II contradicts the statement, which says the meeting will be held one way or the other.
Answer: (A).

q:
Statement: Every train that stops at Rampur also stops at Shantinagar. No express train stops at Shantinagar. The 10:15 train stops at Rampur.
Conclusions:
I. The 10:15 train is not an express train.
II. The 10:15 train stops at Shantinagar.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
Stops at Rampur ⇒ stops at Shantinagar, so the 10:15 stops at Shantinagar (II).
Express ⇒ does not stop at Shantinagar; contrapositive: stops at Shantinagar ⇒ not express. So the 10:15 is not an express (I).
Answer: (C).

q:
A company claims that its new fertiliser raises wheat yields, because farms that used it this season produced 20% more wheat per hectare than they did last season.
Which of the following, if true, weaken the company's claim? (Select all that apply.)
options: The farms that used the fertiliser also switched to a new high-yield seed variety this season.
Yields were unchanged on neighbouring farms with similar soil and weather that did not use the fertiliser.
The new fertiliser costs more than the fertilisers used earlier.
Rainfall this season was far better than last season, and yields also rose by about 20% on farms that did not use the fertiliser.
solution:
(D): better rain explains the rise, and non-users rose just as much, so the fertiliser need not be the cause.
(A): a second change (seed) on the same farms is an alternative cause.
(B) rules out weather and soil, so it strengthens the claim.
(C) is about cost, not yield; irrelevant.

q:
"Every doctor at City Hospital has at least ten years of experience." Dr. Rao is a doctor at City Hospital.
Which one of the following follows logically?
options: Every doctor with ten years of experience works at City Hospital.
Dr. Rao has at least ten years of experience.
Dr. Rao is the most experienced doctor at City Hospital.
Dr. Rao has exactly ten years of experience.
solution:
All City Hospital doctors have ≥ 10 years; Dr. Rao is one of them: (B).
(D) turns "at least" into "exactly".
(A) is the converse.
(C) is not stated.

q:
Statement: In a class of 50 students, 30 passed in Mathematics and 35 passed in Science.
Conclusions:
I. At least 15 students passed in both subjects.
II. At most 15 students failed in both subjects.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
Let $b$ = passed both. Passed at least one $=65-b \le 50$, so $b\ge15$: I follows.
Failed both $=50-(65-b)=b-15$. Since $b\le30$ (only 30 passed Maths), failed both $\le 15$: II follows.
Answer: (C).

q:
Statement: Some of the volunteers are teachers. Every teacher in the group attended the training.
Conclusions:
I. Some volunteers attended the training.
II. All the volunteers attended the training.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
The volunteers who are teachers attended the training, so some volunteers did: I follows.
Nothing is said about volunteers who are not teachers, so II does not follow.
Answer: (A).

q:
"To reduce absenteeism, the company will pay a bonus to every employee who takes no unplanned leave in a quarter."
Which one of the following is an assumption on which the company's plan depends?
options: Absenteeism is the company's most serious problem.
Employees will also take less planned leave.
Every employee wants to earn the bonus.
At least some unplanned leave taken by employees is within their control.
solution:
A reward can change behaviour only if the behaviour can be changed. If all unplanned leave were unavoidable (illness, emergencies), the bonus could not reduce it. Negating (D) defeats the plan.
(C) is too strong; "some" employees responding is enough.
(A) is not needed.
(B) is irrelevant; the plan targets unplanned leave.

q:
After a city opened several new police stations, the number of thefts reported in the city rose, although officials believe that the actual number of thefts fell.
Which one of the following, if true, best reconciles these two claims?
options: The new police stations were opened in areas that had few thefts.
With a police station now close by, many victims who earlier did not bother to report small thefts now report them.
Many thieves moved to neighbouring cities after the stations opened.
Police officers for the new stations were transferred from other cities.
solution:
Reported thefts = actual thefts × share reported. If the reporting share rose enough, reports can rise while thefts fall: (B).
(A) does not explain any rise in reports.
(C) explains a fall in thefts but not the rise in reports.
(D) is irrelevant.

q:
Label on a medicine: "Take this tablet only after meals."
Which one of the following is an assumption implicit in this instruction?
options: Patients eat exactly three meals a day.
The tablet is very expensive.
Taking the tablet on an empty stomach may be harmful or less effective.
The tablet cures all stomach ailments.
solution:
The instruction restricts the timing; that is sensible only if the timing matters, i.e. an empty stomach is worse: (C).
(B) and (D) are irrelevant to timing.
(A) is not needed; the instruction applies to whatever meals are taken.

q:
Statement: Mohan said, "I will attend the wedding only if my leave is approved." Mohan did not attend the wedding.
Conclusions:
I. Mohan's leave was not approved.
II. Mohan's leave was approved.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
"Attend only if leave approved" means attend ⇒ approved. Not attending tells us nothing about approval: his leave may have been approved and he still stayed away, or it may have been refused. Neither I nor II is certain.
Answer: (D).
Trap: reading "only if" as "if".

q:
Statement: Everyone who passed the written test was called for an interview. Some of those called for an interview were not selected. Pooja was selected.
Conclusions:
I. Pooja passed the written test.
II. Pooja was called for an interview.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
The statements never say that only those who passed the test (or only those interviewed) could be selected. "Passed ⇒ interviewed" says nothing about how a selected candidate got there. So neither I nor II is certain.
Answer: (D).
Trap: assuming the usual recruitment process instead of reading only what is stated.

q:
Researchers found that people who live near parks report better mental health than people who do not. They concluded that access to green space improves mental health.
Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens their conclusion?
options: People in good mental health prefer to live near parks.
When new parks were built in some neighbourhoods, residents' mental-health scores rose compared with similar neighbourhoods that got no park.
Houses near parks cost more, so their residents tend to be wealthier.
Most parks in the city are maintained by the municipality.
solution:
A before-and-after comparison against similar neighbourhoods isolates the park as the cause: (B).
(A) reverses the causation and weakens.
(C) offers an alternative cause (wealth) and weakens.
(D) is irrelevant.

q:
"If a number is divisible by 6, it is divisible by 3." The number N is not divisible by 3.
Which one of the following follows logically?
options: N is divisible by 2.
N is an odd number.
N is not divisible by 6.
N is divisible by 6 but not by 2.
solution:
Contrapositive of "6 | N ⇒ 3 | N" is "3 ∤ N ⇒ 6 ∤ N": (C).
(A) and (B) cannot be decided (N could be 4 or 5).
(D) contradicts the conclusion.

q:
Print sales of a newspaper fell by 20% in the six months after it raised its price from ₹5 to ₹8. The editor concludes that the price rise caused the fall.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the editor's conclusion?
options: In the same six months, print sales of rival newspapers that kept their prices unchanged also fell by about 20%.
Many readers wrote letters complaining about the new price.
The newspaper's revenue from print sales rose despite the fall in copies sold.
Sales of the newspaper's online edition rose in the same period.
solution:
If papers that did not raise prices lost the same 20%, something common to all papers explains the fall, not the price rise: (A).
(B) supports the editor.
(D) is consistent with either explanation.
(C) concerns revenue, not the cause of the fall in copies.

q:
"You need not have brought an umbrella," Asha said to Ravi.
Based only on this sentence, which one of the following can be inferred?
options: Ravi left his umbrella at home.
Asha had asked Ravi to bring an umbrella.
Ravi did not bring an umbrella.
Ravi brought an umbrella, which turned out to be unnecessary.
solution:
"Need not have + past participle" refers to something that was done but was unnecessary: Ravi did bring it: (D).
(C) and (A) contradict this. ("Did not need to bring" could mean he did not bring it; "need not have brought" cannot.)
(B) is not implied.

q:
Advertisement: "Wanted: a cook who can prepare South Indian dishes. Apply with references."
Which one of the following is an assumption implicit in the advertisement?
options: Cooks without references are dishonest.
References may help the employer judge whether an applicant is suitable.
The employer does not know how to cook.
Only people from South India may apply.
solution:
Asking for references makes sense only if they help in judging applicants: (B).
(D) confuses a cuisine with a place of origin.
(A) is far too strong.
(C) is not needed; people hire cooks for many reasons.

q:
"All the rooms on the second floor of the hostel are air-conditioned. Some air-conditioned rooms have attached bathrooms." Room 204 is on the second floor.
Which of the following must be true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Room 204 has an attached bathroom.
Some air-conditioned rooms are on the second floor.
Some rooms on the second floor have attached bathrooms.
Room 204 is air-conditioned.
solution:
(D): second floor ⇒ air-conditioned.
(B): room 204 is an air-conditioned room on the second floor.
(A) and (C) fail: the air-conditioned rooms with bathrooms may all be on other floors.

q:
In a survey of a city's commuters, 60% use the metro at least once a week, 50% use buses at least once a week, and 20% use neither.
Based only on this information, which one of the following is correct?
options: 30% of the commuters use both the metro and buses at least once a week.
40% of the commuters use only the metro.
10% of the commuters use both the metro and buses at least once a week.
More commuters use only buses than use both.
solution:
At least one $=100-20=80\%$. Both $=60+50-80=30\%$: (A).
(C) forgets the 20% who use neither ($60+50-100$).
Only metro $=60-30=30\%$, so (B) is false.
Only buses $=50-30=20\%$, which is less than 30%, so (D) is false.

q:
"No reptile in the zoo is kept outdoors." The python is a reptile in the zoo.
Which one of the following follows logically?
options: No animal in the zoo is kept outdoors.
Every animal kept indoors in the zoo is a reptile.
The python is kept in a glass enclosure.
The python is not kept outdoors.
solution:
Reptile in the zoo ⇒ not outdoors; the python is one: (D).
(B) is the converse.
(C) adds a detail not given.
(A) over-generalises from reptiles to all animals.

q:
Statement: Some laptops sold by the shop are refurbished. Every refurbished laptop sold by the shop carries a six-month warranty.
Conclusions:
I. Some laptops sold by the shop carry a six-month warranty.
II. Any laptop sold by the shop that does not carry a six-month warranty is not refurbished.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
I: the refurbished laptops (some exist) carry the warranty, so some laptops do: follows.
II: contrapositive of "refurbished ⇒ warranty": follows.
Answer: (C).

q:
"Our school will cut its paper use by half this year by asking teachers to set all homework online instead of on printed sheets."
Which one of the following is an assumption on which this claim depends?
options: Every student owns a smartphone.
Teachers prefer setting homework online.
Printed homework sheets account for at least half of the school's paper use.
Online homework improves students' learning.
solution:
Removing homework sheets can halve paper use only if those sheets are at least half of it. Negate (C) (sheets are, say, 30% of use) and the target cannot be met even with full compliance.
(A) is far stronger than needed and is about devices, not paper.
(D) and (B) are irrelevant to the amount of paper saved.

q:
A town's hospital treated more cases of heatstroke this summer than last summer, even though the average temperature this summer was slightly lower.
Which one of the following, if true, best explains this?
options: This summer had several short spells of extreme heat, while last summer's heat was steadier and never reached such peaks.
The hospital employed more doctors this summer than last summer.
The average temperature last summer was higher than this summer.
Heatstroke is more common among older people than among younger people.
solution:
An average can fall while the peaks rise. Heatstroke is driven by extreme heat, so a few severe spells explain more cases despite a lower average: (A).
(B) does not explain more cases.
(D) would explain a difference only if the town's age profile had changed, which is not stated.
(C) merely restates the puzzle.

q:
"Whenever it is raining in the morning, Kavya takes the bus to work." This morning, Kavya walked to work.
Which one of the following follows logically?
options: Kavya walks to work whenever it is not raining.
Kavya dislikes travelling by bus.
It rained in the evening.
It was not raining this morning.
solution:
Rain in the morning ⇒ bus. She did not take the bus, so it was not raining this morning: (D).
(A) is the inverse of the rule, not implied.
(B) and (C) are out of scope.

q:
"If the shop is open, its lights are on. Its lights are off. So the shop is closed."
Which one of the following arguments has the same logical form?
options: If the dam's gates are opened, the river rises. The gates were not opened. So the river has not risen.
If the dam's gates are opened, the river rises. The river has not risen. So the gates were not opened.
The river rises only when it rains. It rained. So the river rose.
If the dam's gates are opened, the river rises. The river has risen. So the gates were opened.
solution:
The given argument is "If P then Q; not Q; so not P" (valid, denying the consequent). (B) has exactly this form.
(D) affirms the consequent; (A) denies the antecedent (both invalid).
(C) treats a necessary condition as sufficient.

q:
"In an office, every employee who works on Saturday gets the following Monday off. Some employees who get Monday off are in the sales team." Ankit works this Saturday.
Which of the following must be true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every employee who gets Monday off works on Saturday.
Ankit is in the sales team.
Some employees who get Monday off work on Saturday.
Ankit gets the following Monday off.
solution:
(D): works Saturday ⇒ Monday off.
(C): Ankit himself is such an employee.
(B) fails: the sales-team members with Monday off need not include Ankit.
(A) is the converse of the rule.

q:
Statement: A club has 40 members, of whom 25 are men. More than half of the members attended the annual meeting.
Conclusions:
I. At least one man attended the meeting.
II. At least one woman attended the meeting.
Based only on the statement, which of the conclusions logically follow(s)?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
solution:
At least 21 members attended. There are only 15 women, so at least $21-15=6$ attendees were men: I follows.
All 21 or more attendees could have been men (25 men exist), so II does not follow.
Answer: (A).

q:
A city plans to reduce littering on its beach by placing more dustbins along it.
Which one of the following, if true, most supports the expectation that the plan will succeed?
options: The dustbins on the beach are emptied only once a week.
The number of visitors to the beach has increased this year.
Littering is also a serious problem in the city's parks.
Most people who litter on the beach say they do so because no dustbin is close by.
solution:
The plan works if the lack of nearby bins is the cause of littering: (D).
(A) suggests bins may overflow, which undermines the plan.
(C) is irrelevant to the beach.
(B) does not bear on whether more bins reduce littering.

q:
"All the books on Leela's shelf are novels." The book on the table is not a novel.
Which one of the following follows logically?
options: The book on the table belongs to someone other than Leela.
The book on the table is not from Leela's shelf.
All novels in the house are on Leela's shelf.
Leela does not read anything but novels.
solution:
On Leela's shelf ⇒ novel. Not a novel ⇒ not from her shelf: (B).
(D) confuses what is on the shelf with what she reads.
(C) is the converse.
(A) goes too far: it may be Leela's, just not kept on her shelf.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: As he stepped towards the coach, the ticket checker asked to see his ticket.
Q: He searched every pocket, but the ticket was nowhere to be found.
R: Finally, he remembered that he had left it on the table at home.
S: Ramesh reached the station just as the train pulled in.
options: SQPR
PSQR
SPQR
SPRQ
solution:
S names Ramesh and sets the scene; P ("he", the checker asks for the ticket) follows; Q (he searches his pockets) responds to the request; R ("Finally, he remembered") closes.
(B) starts with "he" before Ramesh is named. (A) has him search before anyone asks for the ticket. (D) puts "Finally, he remembered" before the search it concludes.
Order: SPQR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: This vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds.
Q: The sun heats the water in oceans, lakes and rivers, turning some of it into vapour.
R: The water then flows back through rivers into the sea, and the cycle begins again.
S: When the droplets grow heavy enough, they fall as rain or snow.
options: QPSR
QPRS
PQSR
QSPR
solution:
Follow the process: Q (evaporation) → P ("This vapour" condenses) → S ("the droplets" fall) → R (water returns, "the cycle begins again").
(C) opens with "This vapour", which has nothing to point back to. (D) mentions "the droplets" before they are formed. (B) restarts the cycle before the rain falls.
Order: QPSR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: With the loan, she bought two sewing machines and hired a helper.
Q: Encouraged by her steady income, a local bank offered her a small loan.
R: Lakshmi had been stitching blouses for her neighbours on a borrowed machine for years.
S: Within a year, her earnings had grown enough to repay the bank in full.
options: QRPS
RQPS
RQSP
RPQS
solution:
R introduces Lakshmi; Q the bank offers a loan; P "With the loan" she expands; S she repays "within a year".
(D) uses "the loan" before any loan is offered. (A) opens with "her steady income" before Lakshmi is introduced. (C) has her repay the loan before using it.
Order: RQPS.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Before it, every book had to be copied by hand, a task that could take a scribe many months.
Q: With movable type, hundreds of identical copies could be produced in the time a scribe took to finish one.
R: The printing press changed the way knowledge travelled.
S: As a result, ideas could now spread across a continent within a few years rather than a few generations.
options: PRQS
RPSQ
RPQS
RQPS
solution:
R states the topic; P ("Before it") describes the earlier situation; Q gives the change brought by movable type; S ("As a result") gives the consequence of that change.
(A) opens with "Before it", which has no referent. (B) places "As a result … ideas could now spread" right after hand-copying, which slowed ideas down. (D) places "Before it" after movable type, so "it" would wrongly point to movable type and the speed-up would follow the slow method.
Order: RPQS.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Sunlight and waves break them into ever smaller fragments, but never make them vanish.
Q: Most of these plastics do not decay like paper or wood.
R: Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic waste are washed into the oceans.
S: These fragments, known as microplastics, are swallowed by fish and enter the food chain.
options: RSQP
RQPS
QRPS
RQSP
solution:
R introduces plastic waste; Q ("these plastics") do not decay; P they are broken into "fragments"; S ("These fragments") enter the food chain.
(C) opens with "these plastics". (A) and (D) mention "These fragments" before any fragments have been introduced.
Order: RQPS.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Those who did own one used it sparingly, because every roll of film cost money to buy and develop.
Q: Only a few decades ago, a good camera was an expensive possession that most families could not afford.
R: The result is that ordinary people now take more photographs in a week than their grandparents took in a lifetime.
S: Today, a phone in the pocket of a schoolchild takes better pictures than many of those cameras did.
options: QPSR
QPRS
QSPR
SQPR
solution:
Q sets the past; P ("Those who did own one") continues it; S ("Today") gives the contrast; R ("The result") gives the consequence.
(C) puts "Those who did own one" after the phone sentence, where "one" would wrongly refer to a phone. (D) opens with "those cameras" before cameras are mentioned. (B) states "The result" before the change that causes it.
Order: QPSR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: There, on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, she performs a "waggle dance", repeatedly running in a straight line while shaking her body.
Q: The angle of the run, measured from the vertical, tells the other bees the direction of the food relative to the sun.
R: Guided by these two pieces of information, her sisters can fly straight to flowers they have never seen.
S: Its duration, meanwhile, indicates how far away the food is.
T: When a forager bee finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive to share the news.
options: TPQRS
TQPSR
TPQSR
PTQSR
solution:
T introduces the forager; P ("There", in the hive) describes the dance and its straight run; Q "the run" gives direction; S ("Its duration, meanwhile") gives distance; R ("these two pieces of information") sums up.
(B) mentions "the run" before the dance is described. (D) opens with "There", which needs the hive first. (A) refers to "these two pieces of information" when only one has been given.
Order: TPQSR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Its lid was stuck, and she had to use a knife to prise it open.
Q: While cleaning the attic, Anita came across a small wooden box.
R: When she opened it, she found a letter written by her grandmother fifty years ago.
S: The letter described the day her grandmother had first arrived in the city.
options: QPSR
QPRS
PQRS
QRPS
solution:
Q names Anita and the box; P ("Its lid") is about the box; R she opens it and finds a letter; S ("The letter") describes it.
(D) has her open the box before finding the lid stuck. (C) opens with "Its lid". (A) mentions "The letter" before it is found.
Order: QPRS.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: But the comparison is misleading.
Q: Measured by the cost of moving one person one kilometre, the metro often comes out cheaper.
R: A single metro line can carry tens of thousands of passengers an hour in each direction.
S: A road lane, by contrast, carries only a few thousand vehicles an hour, many with just one occupant.
T: Critics often point out that a new metro line costs many times more per kilometre than a new road.
options: TRPSQ
PTRSQ
TPRSQ
TPSRQ
solution:
T states the critics' claim; P ("But the comparison") rejects it; R metro capacity; S ("by contrast") road capacity; Q the fairer measure and conclusion.
(A) separates "the comparison is misleading" from the comparison it refers to. (D) puts "by contrast" before the thing it contrasts with. (B) opens with "But".
Order: TPRSQ.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: In many parts of India, villages have long protected small patches of forest dedicated to local deities.
Q: As a result, they now shelter plants and animals that have vanished from the surrounding countryside.
R: Botanists, who once ignored these groves as too small to matter, now study them closely.
S: Because cutting even a twig from them was forbidden, these groves have survived while the forests around them were cleared.
options: PSQR
RPSQ
PSRQ
SPQR
solution:
P introduces the protected patches; S ("these groves") explains their survival; Q ("As a result") gives the consequence; R explains why botanists now study them.
(D) opens with "these groves". (C) places "As a result, they now shelter plants" after the botanists, so "they" and the cause no longer fit. (B) opens with "these groves".
Order: PSQR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: First, bring a cup of water to the boil in a small pan.
Q: Finally, strain the tea into a cup and add sugar to taste.
R: Then pour in the milk and heat the mixture until it rises.
S: Once the water boils, add the tea leaves and let them simmer for a minute.
options: SPRQ
PSRQ
PRSQ
PSQR
solution:
Sequence words decide it: P "First" → S "Once the water boils" → R "Then" → Q "Finally".
(A) adds leaves to boiling water before the water is boiled. (C) adds milk before the tea leaves, contradicting "Once the water boils". (D) strains the tea before the milk is added, leaving "Finally" in the middle.
Order: PSRQ.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: A fever is not itself a disease but one of the body's ways of fighting an infection.
Q: For this reason, doctors do not always rush to bring down a mild fever.
R: Many of the bacteria and viruses that cause infections multiply best at normal body temperature.
S: By raising its temperature by a degree or two, the body slows them down and speeds up the work of its own defence cells.
options: QPRS
PSRQ
PRSQ
SPRQ
solution:
P gives the claim; R introduces the bacteria and viruses; S ("slows them down") explains the mechanism; Q ("For this reason") draws the practical conclusion.
(B) has "them" with no plural noun to refer to. (A) opens with "For this reason". (D) opens with "slows them down".
Order: PRSQ.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Yet the system works with remarkably few errors, using nothing more than a simple code of colours and letters painted on each lid.
Q: The lunch boxes are collected from homes, sorted at railway stations and carried by train and bicycle to their destinations.
R: Every morning, in a large Indian city, thousands of home-cooked lunches travel from kitchens to offices.
S: Each box passes through the hands of three or four carriers before it reaches its owner.
options: RQSP
PRQS
QRSP
RPQS
solution:
R introduces the lunches; Q describes the route; S stresses how many hands each box passes through; P ("Yet … few errors") contrasts the complexity with the accuracy.
(C) opens with "The lunch boxes" before the lunches are introduced. (D) says "Yet the system works" before any system or difficulty has been described. (B) opens with "Yet".
Order: RQSP.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: He decided to sell it at the weekly market in the next village.
Q: On the way, a trader offered him a goat in exchange for the cow, and he agreed.
R: By evening, he had traded the goat for a hen, and the hen for a handful of beans.
S: A farmer once owned a cow that gave very little milk.
options: SQPR
PSQR
SPQR
SPRQ
solution:
S introduces the farmer and the cow; P ("He decided to sell it"); Q ("On the way" to the market) he swaps the cow for a goat; R ("By evening") the further swaps.
(B) opens with "He … it". (A) has him "on the way" before deciding to go anywhere. (D) trades "the goat" before he has one.
Order: SPQR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Modern filters therefore learn from millions of messages that users mark as spam, instead of relying on fixed lists of words.
Q: Spammers responded by misspelling those words, writing "l0ttery" or "pr1ze".
R: Unwanted bulk email, or spam, once made up the majority of all email sent.
S: Early filters simply blocked messages containing certain words, such as "lottery" or "prize".
options: RQSP
RSQP
SRQP
RPSQ
solution:
R defines the problem; S the first response (word lists); Q spammers "responded by misspelling those words"; P ("therefore") the modern answer.
(C) opens with "Early filters" before saying what is being filtered. (A) mentions "those words" before any words are listed. (D) places "therefore" before the reason for the change (misspelling) is given.
Order: RSQP.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Soon afterwards, three tiny eggs appeared in it.
Q: Each day they wove the pieces together more tightly.
R: Two sparrows began to carry twigs and straw to a corner of our balcony.
S: Within a week, the nest was complete.
options: QRSP
RQPS
RQSP
RSQP
solution:
R introduces the sparrows; Q ("they wove") the building; S ("Within a week") the finished nest; P ("Soon afterwards") the eggs.
(D) finishes the nest before the weaving. (A) opens with "they". (B) puts eggs "in it" before the nest is complete.
Order: RQSP.

q:
Three of the following four sentences form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does NOT belong to it.
P: Solar panels were first used to power satellites in space.
Q: On sunny days, any surplus can be fed into the grid, earning the household a credit.
R: Over the panels' lifetime, these credits can repay much of their initial cost.
S: Rooftop solar panels let households generate part of their own electricity.
options: P
Q
R
S
solution:
Sentences S, Q and R form a chain about household economics: own electricity → surplus earns "a credit" → "these credits" repay the cost. Sentence P is a historical aside about satellites that connects to none of them.
Answer: sentence P.

q:
Choose the sentence that most appropriately completes the paragraph.
"Many people assume that a desert is a place without life. In fact, deserts are home to a remarkable range of plants and animals. ________"
options: Many deserts are becoming hotter every decade.
Most of them survive by being active at night and by storing water whenever it is available.
The largest hot desert in the world lies in Africa.
Deserts cover about one-third of the earth's land surface.
solution:
The paragraph has just claimed that deserts hold many plants and animals; the natural next step explains how "they" manage to live there: (B) ("Most of them" refers back to the plants and animals).
(D), (A) and (C) are facts about deserts as places and drop the thread about life.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: She practised every evening after school, even during the holidays.
Q: Divya joined her school's chess club when she was nine.
R: Three years later, she won the district championship.
S: At first, she lost almost every game she played.
options: SQPR
QPSR
QSPR
QRSP
solution:
Q names Divya; S ("At first") the early failures; P the effort; R ("Three years later") the result.
(B) puts "At first" after the practice. (A) opens with "she". (D) jumps "Three years later" before "At first".
Order: QSPR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: The saver's balance is larger at the end of the year, but it buys about 2 percent less than before.
Q: Suppose prices rise by 6 percent in a year while a savings account pays 4 percent interest.
R: This is why economists distinguish between the nominal return on savings and the real return, which allows for rising prices.
S: Money kept in a bank can lose value even while the balance grows.
options: SQPR
SPQR
SQRP
QSPR
solution:
S states the paradox; Q ("Suppose") sets up the example; P works out the example (6% − 4% ≈ 2% less); R ("This is why") draws the general lesson.
(D) splits the example (Q and P) with the general claim in between. (B) refers to "The saver's balance" before the example is set up. (C) draws the lesson before the example is finished.
Order: SQPR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Most had died in the dry months because nobody had been assigned to water them.
Q: The drive was widely reported as a great success.
R: Last monsoon, volunteers planted ten thousand saplings along the highway in a single day.
S: A year later, an inspection found that fewer than a third of the saplings were still alive.
options: RSQP
RQSP
RQPS
QRSP
solution:
R the planting; Q ("The drive") the praise at the time; S ("A year later") the inspection; P ("Most had died") explains the inspection's finding.
(A) reports the praise after the inspection, breaking the time order. (C) explains the deaths before they are discovered. (D) opens with "The drive".
Order: RQSP.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: The headmistress decided to collect the rainwater that fell on the school's large roof.
Q: Pipes now carry the water from the roof into an underground tank, and the overflow is led into a pit that recharges the borewell.
R: Every summer, the school's borewell ran dry and water had to be bought from tankers.
S: She persuaded the parents' association to pay for the pipes and the tank.
T: Last summer, for the first time in a decade, the school did not need a single tanker.
options: RSPQT
PRSQT
RPSQT
RPQST
solution:
R the problem; P the headmistress's decision; S ("She persuaded") the funding; Q ("now carry") the working system; T ("Last summer") the result.
(B) opens with the decision before the problem it solves. (A) has "She" before the headmistress is mentioned. (D) describes the installed system before anyone has paid for it.
Order: RPSQT.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Each student in the front row received one piece.
Q: He folded it in half three times.
R: The teacher took a large square sheet of paper.
S: Then he cut the paper along the folds into eight equal pieces.
options: RQSP
QRSP
RSQP
RQPS
solution:
R introduces the teacher and the sheet; Q ("He folded it"); S ("Then … along the folds") cuts; P hands out "one piece".
(C) cuts "along the folds" before folding. (B) opens with "He … it". (D) hands out pieces before cutting.
Order: RQSP.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Since a pipeline brought water to every lane last year, the walk has shrunk to a few minutes.
Q: Such savings of time rarely appear in the accounts of water projects, yet they may be their largest benefit.
R: The hours saved are now spent on paid work, on children's homework, or simply on rest.
S: In the old days, women in the village spent up to three hours a day fetching water from a distant well.
options: SRPQ
SQPR
SPRQ
PSRQ
solution:
S the old burden; P the pipeline ("the walk has shrunk"); R ("The hours saved") what is done with the time; Q ("Such savings of time") the general point.
(A) speaks of "hours saved" before anything has been saved. (D) opens with "the walk" before any walk is mentioned. (B) refers to "Such savings of time" before the pipeline that creates them.
Order: SPRQ.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: A password alone is a weak lock, because it can be guessed, stolen or reused.
Q: This is why banks warn customers never to share such codes with anyone, even a caller who claims to be from the bank.
R: The protection is not perfect, however; criminals sometimes trick users into reading out the code over the phone.
S: Even if a thief learns the password, he cannot log in without that code.
T: Two-factor authentication adds a second requirement: a one-time code sent to the user's phone.
options: PTSQR
PTSRQ
TPSRQ
PSTRQ
solution:
P the problem; T the remedy (a one-time code); S ("that code") why it helps; R ("however") its weakness, tricking users into reading out the code; Q ("This is why … never to share") the warning that follows from that weakness.
(D) mentions "that code" before any code is introduced. (C) opens with the remedy before the problem it fixes. (A) gives the warning against sharing codes before the trickery that makes it necessary, and leaves "however" dangling at the end.
Order: PTSRQ.

q:
Choose the sentence that most appropriately completes the paragraph.
"A good map leaves things out. A map that showed every tree, every lamp post and every pothole would be as large and as confusing as the city itself. ________"
options: Paper maps are rapidly being replaced by apps on phones.
Many cities have more potholes than lamp posts.
Most modern maps are prepared from satellite photographs.
Its usefulness comes precisely from the mapmaker's decisions about what to omit.
solution:
The paragraph argues that leaving things out is what makes a map good; the closing sentence should complete that argument: (D).
(C) and (A) change the subject to how maps are made or used.
(B) seizes on a detail (potholes) and drops the point.

q:
Three of the following four sentences form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does NOT belong to it.
P: A warm patch of water in the Pacific, for instance, can weaken rainfall over India months later.
Q: Farmers in many regions still sow their crops according to traditional calendars.
R: Forecasters therefore watch sea temperatures across several oceans long before the rains are due.
S: Forecasting the monsoon is difficult because it depends on conditions over oceans thousands of kilometres away.
options: P
Q
R
S
solution:
S (difficulty: distant oceans) → P ("for instance", an example) → R ("therefore", what forecasters do) form a chain about forecasting. Q is about farmers' sowing practice and links to none of them.
Answer: sentence Q.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Arun bought a torch from the shop near his house.
Q: The shopkeeper apologised and gave him a new one.
R: When he reached home and switched it on, it did not work.
S: The next morning, he took it back to the shop.
options: PSRQ
RPSQ
PRQS
PRSQ
solution:
P the purchase; R it fails at home; S ("The next morning") he returns it; Q the shopkeeper replaces it.
(A) has him take the torch back before finding the fault. (B) opens with "he … it". (C) has the shopkeeper replace the torch before Arun returns to the shop.
Order: PRSQ.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: The moon produces no light of its own.
Q: As the moon moves along its orbit, we see more or less of its sunlit half.
R: These changing views give rise to the familiar phases, from new moon to full moon and back.
S: What we call moonlight is sunlight reflected from its surface.
options: PSRQ
PSQR
PQSR
SPQR
solution:
P the claim; S explains moonlight; Q the moon's motion changes how much sunlit half we see; R ("These changing views") names the result.
(D) opens with "its surface", which has no referent. (C) puts the moonlight sentence between Q and "These changing views", which then has nothing to point to. (A) uses "These changing views" before any change is described.
Order: PSQR.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: The guard at the gate told her that visitors were not allowed after six.
Q: The guard hesitated, looked at the flask, and then quietly opened the gate.
R: Rekha reached the hospital at a quarter past six, carrying a flask of soup for her father.
S: Ten minutes later, she came out smiling and thanked him as she left.
T: She explained that her father had not eaten all day and that she would stay only five minutes.
options: RPQTS
RTPQS
RPTQS
PRTQS
solution:
R names Rekha and the time; P the guard refuses; T she explains; Q he relents; S ("Ten minutes later") she leaves.
(B) has her explain before being refused. (D) opens with "her" before Rekha is named. (A) has the guard open the gate before hearing her reason.
Order: RPTQS.

q:
The first and the last sentences of a paragraph are given as 1 and 6. Choose the option that gives the most coherent order of the four sentences in between.
1: A good bridge must be strong enough to carry the heaviest load that will ever cross it.
P: Wind, for example, can make a long bridge sway, and a sway that keeps time with the gusts can grow larger and larger.
Q: It must also cope with forces that are easy to overlook.
R: Heat is another such force, since steel expands on a hot afternoon and contracts at night.
S: Engineers leave small gaps, called expansion joints, so that this daily stretching does not crack the structure.
6: Strength, in short, is only the first of many demands on a bridge's designer.
options: PQRS
QRPS
QPSR
QPRS
solution:
After 1 (strength for the heaviest load), Q ("also … forces that are easy to overlook") opens the new point; P ("Wind, for example") is the first such force; R ("another such force") the second; S ("this daily stretching") follows heat; 6 sums up.
(B) calls heat "another such force" before any force has been named. (A) gives "Wind, for example" before the claim it illustrates. (C) refers to "this daily stretching" before heat is mentioned.
Order: QPRS.

q:
Three of the following four sentences form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does NOT belong to it.
P: Marathon runners often train for months before a race.
Q: Walking briskly for thirty minutes a day lowers the risk of heart disease.
R: It also helps control weight and improves mood.
S: Unlike most forms of exercise, it needs no special equipment or training.
options: P
Q
R
S
solution:
Q, R ("It also") and S ("it needs no special equipment") all describe the benefits of daily walking. P is about marathon training and does not continue the paragraph.
Answer: sentence P.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Governments, newspapers and traders quickly reorganised their work around this new speed.
Q: The telegraph cut such delays from weeks to minutes.
R: Before the telegraph, a message could travel no faster than the horse or ship that carried it.
S: News of a battle might reach the capital weeks after the battle had been decided.
options: RPSQ
RSQP
QRSP
RQPS
solution:
R the old limit; S an example of the delay; Q ("such delays") the change; P ("this new speed") the consequence.
(C) opens with "such delays". (A) mentions "this new speed" before any speed-up. (D) ends with weeks-long delays after the telegraph has already removed them.
Order: RSQP.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Milk and bread are among the items that shoppers buy most often.
Q: To reach them, a shopper must walk past aisles of other goods.
R: The layout is thus no accident: it is designed to turn a quick errand into a longer visit.
S: Supermarkets usually place them at the back of the store, far from the entrance.
T: Some of these goods, seen on the way, end up in the basket although the shopper never planned to buy them.
options: SPQTR
PSQRT
PSQTR
PQSTR
solution:
P names the items; S ("them") where they are placed; Q ("To reach them") the walk past other goods; T ("these goods") impulse purchases; R ("thus") the conclusion about layout.
(A) opens with "them". (D) has shoppers walk "to reach them" before we know the items are at the back. (B) draws the conclusion and then leaves "these goods" stranded after it.
Order: PSQTR.

q:
Choose the sentence that most appropriately completes the paragraph.
"Ravi set his alarm for five o'clock because his train left at six. When the alarm rang, he switched it off and fell asleep again. ________"
options: The alarm clock had been a gift from his sister.
He reached the station an hour before the train left.
Trains in that city always leave exactly on time.
He woke up at half past six and realised that he had missed the train.
solution:
The story builds to a consequence of falling asleep again; (D) supplies it.
(B) contradicts the set-up (he went back to sleep).
(A) is an irrelevant detail.
(C) is a general remark that leaves the story unresolved.

q:
The four sentences below can be arranged into a coherent paragraph. Which of the following statements about that arrangement are correct? (Select all that apply.)
P: The beetles, however, lived high on the cane stalks, out of the toads' reach.
Q: Instead, the toads ate almost anything else they could catch, and multiplied rapidly.
R: In the 1930s, farmers in one country imported a species of toad to eat the beetles that were damaging their sugar cane.
S: Today they number in the millions and threaten many native animals that try to eat them, since their skin is poisonous.
options: S comes immediately after R.
Q comes immediately after P.
R is the first sentence.
P is the last sentence.
solution:
Coherent order: R (the import, with a date) → P ("however", the beetles were out of reach) → Q ("Instead", what the toads ate) → S ("Today", the result).
So (C) and (B) are true; (A) fails (P follows R); (D) fails (S is last).
Coherent order: RPQS.

q:
The five sentences below can be arranged into a coherent paragraph. Which of the following statements about that arrangement are correct? (Select all that apply.)
P: The early schemes, which relied entirely on trust, collapsed.
Q: Several cities launched public bicycle schemes in the hope of cutting short car trips.
R: Within weeks, many bicycles were missing, and others were found broken or dumped in rivers.
S: The idea was simple: let anyone borrow a bicycle from one dock and return it to any other.
T: Later schemes succeeded by requiring users to register with a card and pay a deposit, so that each bicycle could be traced.
options: T is the second sentence.
R comes immediately before P.
P is the last sentence.
S comes immediately after Q.
solution:
Coherent order: Q (schemes launched) → S ("The idea was simple") → R ("Within weeks", the losses) → P ("The early schemes … collapsed") → T ("Later schemes", the fix).
So (D) and (B) are true; (C) fails (T, not P, is last); (A) fails (S is second).
Coherent order: QSRPT.

q:
The four sentences below form a paragraph when suitably ordered. Which of them can NOT be the opening sentence of the paragraph? (Select all that apply.)
P: These fish are themselves eaten by larger fish, seals and seabirds.
Q: These, in turn, are eaten by small fish.
R: Thus the energy of sunlight passes, step by step, up the ocean food chain.
S: Tiny floating plants in the sea capture sunlight and grow.
options: P
Q
R
S
solution:
An opener must not lean on anything earlier. Q begins with "These, in turn", P with "These fish" and R with "Thus": each points back to an earlier sentence, so none can open. Only S (introducing the floating plants) can.
Answer: Q, P and R; coherent order SQPR.

q:
The four sentences below can be arranged into a coherent paragraph. Which of the following statements about that arrangement are correct? (Select all that apply.)
P: This is because warm air rises and collects just below the ceiling.
Q: Most of the heat escapes through the roof.
R: A house without insulation is costly to heat in winter.
S: A layer of insulation under the roof can therefore cut heating bills considerably.
options: S is immediately followed by Q.
P is immediately followed by S.
Q is immediately followed by P.
R is immediately followed by S.
solution:
Coherent order: R (the problem) → Q (heat escapes through the roof) → P ("This is because", the reason) → S ("therefore", the remedy). "This is because" must follow the fact it explains (Q), and "therefore" must follow the whole explanation.
So (C) and (B) are true; (D) and (A) are false.
Coherent order: RQPS.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: By spring, half the town was arriving late for trains, while the few who owned radios were on time.
Q: In 1905, a merchant paid for a clock tower to be built in the market square.
R: Then, one winter, the clock began to lose a few minutes each week, and nobody noticed.
S: For decades, the whole town set its watches by it.
T: The town council finally hired a clockmaker, whose first discovery was that nobody had oiled the mechanism since 1905.
options: QSRPT
QSRTP
SQRPT
QRSPT
solution:
Q the tower is built; S ("For decades … by it") the town relies on it; R ("Then, one winter") the fault begins; P ("By spring") the consequence; T ("finally") the council acts.
(C) opens with "by it". (D) puts "For decades" after the winter fault, scrambling the time line. (B) has the council "finally" act before any consequence has made the problem visible.
Order: QSRPT.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Within a month, it had grown two new leaves.
Q: Proudly, she showed it to everyone who visited.
R: For her birthday, Nisha received a small potted plant.
S: She watered it every morning and kept it near the window.
options: SRPQ
RSPQ
PRSQ
RPSQ
solution:
R names Nisha and the plant; S her care; P ("Within a month") the growth that care produced; Q her pride.
(D) reports the growth before the care that explains it. (A) opens with "She … it". (C) opens with "it".
Order: RSPQ.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Recovering them safely, however, requires equipment that informal recyclers rarely have.
Q: These contain small amounts of gold, copper and other valuable metals.
R: Every year, millions of old phones and computers are thrown away.
S: Instead, wires are often burnt in the open to extract the copper, releasing toxic smoke.
options: RQSP
RPQS
QRPS
RQPS
solution:
R the discarded devices; Q ("These contain") the metals; P ("Recovering them safely, however") the difficulty; S ("Instead") what happens in practice.
(C) opens with "These". (B) has "Recovering them … however" before the metals are mentioned, so "however" contrasts with nothing. (A) puts "Instead" before the safe method it replaces.
Order: RQPS.

q:
Choose the sentence that most appropriately fills the blank.
"Many students believe that rereading their notes is the best way to prepare for an examination. ________ Testing oneself, by contrast, forces the brain to retrieve information, and each act of retrieval strengthens memory."
options: Testing oneself takes much longer than rereading.
Examinations in most colleges are held twice a year.
Rereading, however, often produces only a feeling of familiarity, not the ability to recall.
Notes should always be written neatly and in full sentences.
solution:
The blank must challenge the belief in rereading so that "Testing oneself, by contrast" has something to contrast with: (C).
(D) and (B) are off the point.
(A) already discusses testing, so the next sentence's "Testing oneself, by contrast" would contrast testing with itself.

q:
Select the option that arranges the following sentences in the most coherent order.
P: Decades later, studies of the ocean floor showed that new crust is constantly formed along mid-ocean ridges, pushing the plates apart.
Q: Few geologists took him seriously, however, because he could not explain what force could move entire continents.
R: He pointed out that the coastlines of Africa and South America fit together like pieces of a puzzle, and that the same fossils appear on both sides of the Atlantic.
S: The missing mechanism had been found, and his idea, in a modified form, became a foundation of modern geology.
T: Early in the twentieth century, a scientist proposed that the continents had once been joined and had slowly drifted apart.
options: TRQPS
RTQPS
TRPQS
TRQSP
solution:
T the proposal; R ("He pointed out") the evidence; Q ("however") the objection: no force; P ("Decades later") the discovery; S ("The missing mechanism had been found") the resolution.
(B) opens with "He". (C) has the mechanism discovered before the objection that it was missing. (D) announces "The missing mechanism had been found" before the discovery is described.
Order: TRQPS.

P: Owls hunt mainly at night.
Q: Their large eyes gather what little light there is.
R: Parrots can imitate human speech.
S: Their soft feathers let them fly almost silently towards their prey.
options: P
Q
R

Q: Each speaker was given three minutes, and the sarpanch kept time by tapping a steel tumbler.
R: Nearly every household sent someone to speak.
S: The panchayat met under the banyan tree to decide where the new well should be dug.
options: RSQP

P: As a result, the cashier never needs to type a price, and the shop's stock records are updated automatically.
Q: A scanner reads this number and looks up the price in the shop's computer.
R: Almost every packaged product carries a barcode: a row of black and white stripes of different widths.
S: The widths encode a number that identifies the product.
options: RQSP
RSPQ
SRQP

solution:
R introduces the barcode; S ("The widths") encode a number; Q ("this number") is read by the scanner; P ("As a result") the benefit.

The first and the last sentences of a paragraph are given as 1 and 6. Choose the option that gives the most coherent order of the four sentences in between.
1: Ants returning from a source of food leave a faint chemical trail behind them.
P: If there are two routes to the same food, ants on the shorter route complete more round trips in the same time.
Q: Over time, the shorter path carries the stronger trail, and most ants end up using it.
R: Their trail is therefore refreshed more often than the trail on the longer route, which slowly fades.
S: Other ants, sensing the trail, follow it to the food and strengthen it on their way back.
6: Engineers have borrowed this idea to design programs that search for short routes through computer networks.
options: SPRQ
SRPQ
PSRQ
SPQR
solution:
After 1 (returning ants leave a trail), S explains how trails are followed and strengthened; P introduces two routes; R ("therefore") follows from more round trips; Q ("Over time") the outcome; 6 refers to "this idea".
(C) separates "therefore" in R from the round-trip fact in P it depends on. (B) says "Their trail is therefore refreshed more often" before the two routes are introduced. (D) states the outcome before the reason for it.
Order: SPRQ.

P: When we rub our hands with soap, these molecules break the film into tiny droplets.
Q: Plain water cannot easily wash away the greasy film on our hands in which germs are trapped.
R: The droplets, along with the germs inside them, are then rinsed away by water.
S: Soap molecules have one end that clings to water and another that clings to grease.
options: QPSR
QSPR
QSRP
PQSR
solution:
Q the problem (a greasy film); S the property of soap molecules; P ("these molecules") break the film; R ("The droplets … then") are rinsed away.
(A) uses "these molecules" before molecules are introduced. (C) rinses "The droplets" before they are formed. (D) opens with "these molecules".
Order: QSPR.
